questions.topic: Types of Solutions and Concentration Terms
questions.question: Which concentration term is temperature-independent?
questions.explanation: Molality is defined using the mass of solvent (mol kg<sup>−1</sup>), and mass does not change with temperature, unlike volume. Molarity, normality, and volume % all involve volume of solution, which expands/contracts with temperature.
questions.hint: Think about which definition uses mass instead of volume.
distractor_logic: Molarity uses volume of solution, which changes with temperature.
Volume percentage is volume-based and hence temperature-sensitive.
Normality also uses volume of solution.

questions.topic: Types of Solutions and Concentration Terms
questions.question: Mole fraction of a component in a solution is defined as:
options: Mass of component ÷ total mass of solution × 100
Moles of component ÷ volume of solution in litres
Moles of component ÷ total mass of solution
Moles of component ÷ total moles of all components
questions.explanation: Mole fraction x<sub>i</sub> = n<sub>i</sub> / (n<sub>1</sub> + n<sub>2</sub> + ...), i.e. moles of that component divided by total moles of all components in the solution.
questions.hint: It is a mole-based ratio, not a mass or volume ratio.
distractor_logic: This describes mass percentage, not mole fraction.
This describes molarity, not mole fraction.
This mixes moles with mass, which is not the definition.

questions.topic: Types of Solutions and Concentration Terms
questions.question: The sum of mole fractions of all components in a solution is always equal to:
options: Depends on the number of components
questions.explanation: By definition, x<sub>1</sub> + x<sub>2</sub> + ... = 1 for any solution, since each x<sub>i</sub> = n<sub>i</sub>/n<sub>total</sub> and the numerators sum to n<sub>total</sub>.
questions.hint: Each mole fraction is a fraction of the whole; fractions of a whole must add to 1.
distractor_logic: Mole fractions cannot sum to zero unless there is no solution at all.
The sum is always exactly 1 regardless of how many components are present.
100 would apply to percentages, not mole fractions (which are unitless ratios).

questions.topic: Types of Solutions and Concentration Terms
questions.question: Parts per million (ppm) is generally used to express the concentration of a solute when it is present:
options: Only when the solute is a gas
In very large amounts, comparable to the solvent
questions.explanation: ppm expresses mass of solute per 10<sup>6</sup> parts of solution and is used for trace-level solutes, e.g. dissolved O<sub>2</sub> in water or pollutants in air, where percentage values would be inconveniently small.
questions.hint: Think about why a millionth-based unit would even be needed.
distractor_logic: ppm is a general trace-concentration unit, not restricted to alloys.
ppm is used for trace solutes of any physical state, not only gases.
For large amounts, mass % or molarity is more convenient.

questions.topic: Types of Solutions and Concentration Terms
questions.question: Molarity of a solution is defined as:
options: Moles of solute per kg of solvent
Grams of solute per litre of solution
Moles of solute per litre of solution
Moles of solute per litre of solvent
questions.explanation: Molarity M = moles of solute / volume of solution in litres (not solvent). It is the most commonly used unit in titrations and volumetric analysis.
questions.hint: Molarity uses volume of the whole solution, not solvent, and moles, not grams.
distractor_logic: This describes molality, which uses mass of solvent.
Molarity uses moles of solute, not grams.
Molarity is based on volume of solution, not volume of solvent.

questions.topic: Types of Solutions and Concentration Terms
questions.question: Which of these concentration units changes in numerical value if the temperature of the solution is raised (solution expands)?
questions.explanation: Molarity = moles of solute / volume of solution (L). As temperature rises, the solution expands, its volume increases, and so molarity decreases even though the amount of solute is unchanged. Mass %, mole fraction, and molality involve only masses/moles and stay constant.
questions.hint: Look for the concentration term with volume of solution in its definition.
distractor_logic: Mass percentage is purely mass-based, unaffected by thermal expansion.
Molality uses mass of solvent, unaffected by thermal expansion.
Mole fraction is a ratio of moles, unaffected by volume changes.

questions.topic: Solubility of Gases in Liquids (Henry's Law)
questions.question: Henry's law relates the partial pressure of a gas above a liquid to:
options: The mole fraction of the dissolved gas in the solution
The molar mass of the solvent
The boiling point of the solvent
The temperature of the liquid only
questions.explanation: Henry's law states p = K<sub>H</sub> · x, where p is the partial pressure of the gas and x is the mole fraction of the gas dissolved in the liquid; K<sub>H</sub> is the Henry's law constant for that gas-solvent pair at a given temperature.
questions.hint: It is a direct proportionality between gas pressure and the amount of gas dissolved.
distractor_logic: Henry's law constant depends on the gas-solvent pair, not simply solvent molar mass.
Boiling point elevation is a separate colligative effect, unrelated to Henry's law.
Temperature affects K<sub>H</sub> but the law itself relates p to dissolved mole fraction.

questions.topic: Solubility of Gases in Liquids (Henry's Law)
questions.question: As temperature increases, the solubility of a gas in a liquid generally:
questions.explanation: For most gases, Henry's law constant K<sub>H</sub> increases with temperature, which (at constant partial pressure) means a smaller mole fraction of gas is needed to reach equilibrium -- i.e. solubility decreases. This is why dissolved O<sub>2</sub> in lakes/rivers falls in summer, harming aquatic life.
questions.hint: Recall why soda goes flat faster when warm, or why fish struggle in warm water.
distractor_logic: K<sub>H</sub> actually increases with temperature for most gases, not decreases.
Solubility decreases with temperature; it does not increase without limit.
Solubility of gases is clearly temperature-dependent, not constant.

questions.topic: Solubility of Gases in Liquids (Henry's Law)
questions.question: A higher value of the Henry's law constant K<sub>H</sub> for a given gas at a fixed temperature indicates that the gas is:
questions.explanation: Since p = K<sub>H</sub>x, for a fixed partial pressure p, a larger K<sub>H</sub> means a smaller mole fraction x is dissolved at equilibrium -- so a higher K<sub>H</sub> corresponds to lower solubility.
questions.hint: Rearrange p = K<sub>H</sub>x to see how x changes when K<sub>H</sub> is large.
distractor_logic: A large K<sub>H</sub> means low solubility, not zero solubility.
This is the reverse of the correct relationship; larger K<sub>H</sub> means less gas dissolves.
Henry's law is precisely about how solubility depends on pressure.

questions.topic: Solubility of Gases in Liquids (Henry's Law)
questions.question: Deep-sea divers are advised to use air diluted with helium (rather than plain compressed air) mainly to avoid:
options: Increased solubility of nitrogen in blood at high pressure causing bends
questions.explanation: At high pressure underwater, Henry's law causes more N<sub>2</sub> to dissolve in blood. If a diver ascends too fast, this dissolved N<sub>2</sub> comes out as bubbles in blood vessels (decompression sickness / 'bends'). Helium is used instead of N<sub>2</sub> because it is much less soluble in blood.
questions.hint: This is the classic NCERT application of Henry's law to diving.
distractor_logic: Cost is not the chemical reason cited in the Henry's law application.
Oxygen toxicity is a separate, secondary concern, not the main reason for using He-O<sub>2</sub> mixtures.
Blood does not freeze at typical diving depths; this is not the reason.

questions.topic: Vapour Pressure of Solutions and Raoult's Law
questions.question: According to Raoult's law, for a solution of two volatile liquids, the partial vapour pressure of each component is:
options: Equal to its pure-liquid vapour pressure regardless of composition
Directly proportional to its mole fraction in solution
Inversely proportional to its mole fraction in solution
Independent of its mole fraction in solution
questions.explanation: Raoult's law: p<sub>i</sub> = x<sub>i</sub>p<sub>i</sub>°, i.e. the partial vapour pressure of each volatile component is directly proportional to its mole fraction in the liquid mixture, with p<sub>i</sub>° being that component's pure vapour pressure.
questions.hint: This is the defining proportionality of Raoult's law.
distractor_logic: p<sub>i</sub> equals p<sub>i</sub>° only when x<sub>i</sub> = 1 (pure liquid), not in general.
The relationship is directly, not inversely, proportional.
Raoult's law explicitly makes p<sub>i</sub> depend on x<sub>i</sub>.

questions.topic: Vapour Pressure of Solutions and Raoult's Law
questions.question: For a solution containing a non-volatile solute, the total vapour pressure of the solution equals:
options: Zero, since the solute is non-volatile
The partial vapour pressure contributed by the solvent alone
The sum of solute and solvent vapour pressures
The vapour pressure of the pure solvent
questions.explanation: A non-volatile solute contributes essentially no vapour pressure of its own, so the total vapour pressure of the solution equals only the partial pressure due to the solvent, p<sub>1</sub> = x<sub>1</sub>p<sub>1</sub>°, which is lower than pure p<sub>1</sub>° because x<sub>1</sub> < 1.
questions.hint: The solute does not evaporate, so it cannot add to vapour pressure.
distractor_logic: The solvent still evaporates, so total vapour pressure is not zero.
The non-volatile solute contributes essentially zero vapour pressure of its own.
It equals x<sub>1</sub>p<sub>1</sub>°, which is less than the pure solvent's vapour pressure p<sub>1</sub>°.

questions.topic: Vapour Pressure of Solutions and Raoult's Law
questions.question: The vapour pressure of a liquid at a given temperature depends on:
options: The strength of intermolecular forces in the liquid
The shape of the container only
questions.explanation: Vapour pressure at a fixed temperature is an intrinsic property arising from the balance between the tendency of molecules to escape (kinetic energy) and the intermolecular forces holding them in the liquid; stronger forces give lower vapour pressure.
questions.hint: Think about why volatile liquids like ether have weak intermolecular forces.
distractor_logic: Vapour pressure is intensive -- it does not depend on how much liquid is present.
Colour is unrelated to the volatility of a liquid.
Container shape has no effect on the equilibrium vapour pressure.

questions.topic: Vapour Pressure of Solutions and Raoult's Law
questions.question: In a solution obeying Raoult's law, if component 1 has a higher pure vapour pressure than component 2 (p<sub>1</sub>° > p<sub>2</sub>°), then component 1 is said to be the more:
questions.explanation: A higher pure vapour pressure at a given temperature means the liquid evaporates more readily, i.e. it is the more volatile component. Vapour pressure and volatility are directly linked.
questions.hint: Higher vapour pressure = molecules escape into vapour more easily = more volatile.
distractor_logic: Viscosity is about resistance to flow, unrelated to vapour pressure ranking.
Density is unrelated to vapour pressure comparisons.
Electronegativity is a property of atoms, not a description of bulk volatility.

questions.topic: Vapour Pressure of Solutions and Raoult's Law
questions.question: The vapour phase above an ideal solution of two volatile liquids is, compared to the liquid phase, relatively richer in:
options: Both components in exactly the same ratio as the liquid
Neither component -- the vapour has a fixed independent composition
questions.explanation: Since the more volatile component has a higher p<sub>i</sub>°, it contributes a larger share of the total vapour pressure relative to its mole fraction, so the vapour phase is enriched in the more volatile component compared with the liquid -- this is the basis of fractional distillation.
questions.hint: This is exactly why fractional distillation can separate volatile liquids.
distractor_logic: If compositions were identical, distillation could never separate the liquids.
Vapour composition is directly determined by the liquid composition via Raoult's law.
It is the more volatile component that concentrates in the vapour.

questions.question: For an ideal solution, the enthalpy of mixing (Δ<sub>mix</sub>H) of the pure components is:
questions.explanation: An ideal solution is defined by obeying Raoult's law over the entire range of concentration, with Δ<sub>mix</sub>H = 0 and Δ<sub>mix</sub>V = 0, because solute-solvent interactions are essentially identical in strength to solute-solute and solvent-solvent interactions.
questions.hint: Ideal mixing involves no net heat change because all interactions are equally strong.
distractor_logic: Negative Δ<sub>mix</sub>H is a feature of solutions with negative deviation, not ideal ones.
Positive Δ<sub>mix</sub>H is a feature of solutions with positive deviation, not ideal ones.
Ideal solutions have a well-defined, predictable Δ<sub>mix</sub>H of exactly zero.

questions.question: Which of these pairs is a classic NCERT example of a nearly ideal solution?
questions.explanation: n-Hexane and n-heptane are structurally very similar non-polar hydrocarbons with nearly identical intermolecular forces, so their mixture closely obeys Raoult's law across the full composition range -- the textbook example of an ideal solution, along with benzene-toluene.
questions.hint: Look for the pair of structurally similar, non-polar hydrocarbons.
distractor_logic: Chloroform-acetone is a standard example of negative deviation, not an ideal solution.
HNO<sub>3</sub>-water shows strong negative deviation and forms a maximum-boiling azeotrope.
Ethanol-acetone is a standard example of positive deviation, not an ideal solution.

questions.question: A solution showing positive deviation from Raoult's law has a total vapour pressure that is:
options: Lower than predicted by Raoult's law
Exactly equal to that predicted by Raoult's law
Higher than predicted by Raoult's law
questions.explanation: In positive deviation, A-B interactions are weaker than A-A and B-B interactions, so molecules escape more easily than in an ideal mixture, making the observed vapour pressure higher than the Raoult's-law prediction (e.g. ethanol-acetone, ethanol-water).
questions.hint: Weaker cross-interactions let molecules escape more easily -- so vapour pressure rises above the ideal line.
distractor_logic: That describes negative deviation, not positive deviation.
Equality with the Raoult's-law prediction describes an ideal solution, not a deviating one.
A deviating solution still has a nonzero, measurable vapour pressure.

questions.question: A minimum-boiling azeotrope, such as the 95.6% ethanol-water mixture, is formed by solutions showing:
options: No relation to Raoult's law deviations
questions.explanation: Solutions with strong positive deviation can reach a composition where the total vapour pressure is a maximum (and hence the boiling point is a minimum) -- this is a minimum-boiling azeotrope, e.g. ethanol-water at 95.6% ethanol by mass.
questions.hint: Higher vapour pressure at some composition corresponds to a lower boiling point there.
distractor_logic: Azeotrope formation is directly a consequence of strong deviation from Raoult's law.
Negative deviation instead produces maximum-boiling azeotropes, e.g. HCl-water.
Ideal solutions obey Raoult's law exactly and do not form azeotropes at all.

questions.question: Mixing chloroform and acetone releases heat and results in contraction of volume. This solution shows:
options: No deviation, since it is exothermic
questions.explanation: Chloroform and acetone form a hydrogen bond between CHCl<sub>3</sub> and the carbonyl oxygen of acetone, making A-B attraction stronger than A-A/B-B attraction. This lowers escaping tendency (Δ<sub>mix</sub>H < 0, Δ<sub>mix</sub>V < 0), giving vapour pressure lower than Raoult's law predicts -- negative deviation.
questions.hint: Stronger cross-interactions (like H-bonding) pull molecules together, lowering vapour pressure below the ideal line.
distractor_logic: Positive deviation involves weaker cross-interactions and volume expansion, the opposite of this case.
Being exothermic is itself evidence of a deviation (negative), not evidence of no deviation.
Ideal solutions have Δ<sub>mix</sub>H = 0 and Δ<sub>mix</sub>V = 0, not exothermic contraction.

questions.question: For a dilute solution of a non-volatile, non-electrolyte solute, the relative lowering of vapour pressure (p<sub>1</sub>° − p<sub>1</sub>)/p<sub>1</sub>° equals:
options: The mole fraction of the solvent, x<sub>1</sub>
The mass fraction of the solvent
The mole fraction of the solute, x<sub>2</sub>
questions.explanation: This is the Raoult-Ostwald relationship: (p<sub>1</sub>° − p<sub>1</sub>)/p<sub>1</sub>° = x<sub>2</sub>, the mole fraction of the (non-volatile) solute, derived directly from Raoult's law since p<sub>1</sub> = x<sub>1</sub>p<sub>1</sub>° and x<sub>1</sub> + x<sub>2</sub> = 1.
questions.hint: This quantity is exactly what defines a colligative property from Raoult's law.
distractor_logic: x<sub>1</sub> (solvent mole fraction) would just reproduce p<sub>1</sub>/p<sub>1</sub>°, not the lowering ratio.
The relation is defined with mole fraction, not mass fraction.
Molarity is a concentration unit; the exact relation here is with mole fraction, not molarity.

questions.question: Relative lowering of vapour pressure is classified as a colligative property because it depends on:
options: The number of solute particles present, not their nature
Only the molar mass of the solvent
The chemical identity of the solute
questions.explanation: Colligative properties depend only on the number (or relative number, i.e. mole fraction) of solute particles in a given amount of solvent, not on what the solute chemically is -- this is precisely why relative lowering of vapour pressure is grouped with boiling point elevation, freezing point depression, and osmotic pressure.
questions.hint: 'Colligative' literally means 'depending on the collection', i.e. count of particles.
distractor_logic: It depends on solute amount relative to solvent, not solvent molar mass alone.
Colour of solute has no bearing on vapour pressure.
Colligative properties are explicitly independent of solute identity.

questions.question: The relative lowering of vapour pressure can be used experimentally to determine:
options: The boiling point of the pure solvent only
The density of the solution only
The molar mass of a non-volatile solute
questions.explanation: Because relative lowering of vapour pressure equals x<sub>2</sub> (mole fraction of solute), measuring p<sub>1</sub>° and p<sub>1</sub> experimentally lets one back-calculate n<sub>2</sub> and hence the molar mass of the dissolved (non-volatile) solute -- a classical application highlighted in NCERT.
questions.hint: This is one of the practical uses of colligative properties mentioned in NCERT.
distractor_logic: Pure solvent boiling point is a known constant, not something this method determines.
Density is not obtained from vapour pressure lowering measurements.
Vapour pressure lowering carries no information about colour.

questions.question: If a non-volatile solute is added to a solvent, the vapour pressure of the resulting solution, compared to the pure solvent, is always:
questions.explanation: Adding a non-volatile solute occupies some of the surface and reduces the mole fraction of solvent (x<sub>1</sub> < 1), so fewer solvent molecules escape into vapour per unit time, lowering the vapour pressure relative to the pure solvent (p<sub>1</sub> = x<sub>1</sub>p<sub>1</sub>° < p<sub>1</sub>°).
questions.hint: Fewer solvent molecules at the surface (diluted by solute) means less evaporation.
distractor_logic: This is the opposite of what actually happens -- vapour pressure decreases, not increases.
Vapour pressure does change; it is not unaffected by adding solute.
The solvent still evaporates to some extent; vapour pressure does not drop to zero.

questions.question: Elevation of boiling point (ΔT<sub>b</sub>) occurs when a non-volatile solute is dissolved because the solution's vapour pressure:
options: Is raised, so a lower temperature reaches 1 atm vapour pressure
Is lowered, so a higher temperature is needed to reach 1 atm vapour pressure
Becomes exactly equal to the solute's own vapour pressure
questions.explanation: Boiling occurs when a liquid's vapour pressure equals atmospheric pressure. Since dissolving a non-volatile solute lowers the solution's vapour pressure at any given temperature, a higher temperature is now needed to raise that vapour pressure back up to 1 atm -- hence elevation of boiling point.
questions.hint: Boiling point is defined by when vapour pressure reaches atmospheric pressure.
distractor_logic: Vapour pressure is lowered by the solute, not raised -- that is why boiling point rises rather than falls.
If vapour pressure were unaffected there would be no boiling point elevation at all.
The solute is non-volatile and contributes essentially no vapour pressure of its own.

questions.question: In the relation ΔT<sub>b</sub> = K<sub>b</sub>m, the quantity K<sub>b</sub> is called the:
questions.explanation: K<sub>b</sub>, the molal elevation constant (also called the ebullioscopic constant), is defined as the boiling point elevation produced by a 1 molal solution of a non-volatile, non-volatile non-electrolyte solute; it is a property of the solvent, with units K kg mol<sup>−1</sup>.
questions.hint: It is defined per unit molality, so it is a 'molal' constant, not molar.
distractor_logic: 'Molar' would relate to molarity (per litre of solution), not molality; K<sub>b</sub> is molal.
The van't Hoff constant (i) is a separate correction factor for dissociation/association.
Henry's law constant K<sub>H</sub> concerns gas solubility, unrelated to boiling point elevation.

questions.question: Boiling point elevation, ΔT<sub>b</sub>, is directly proportional to the solution's:
questions.explanation: ΔT<sub>b</sub> = K<sub>b</sub>m, where m is molality (moles of solute per kg of solvent). Molality is used (rather than molarity) because it does not change with temperature, which matters since boiling point measurements involve heating the solution.
questions.hint: The defining formula for boiling point elevation directly names this quantity.
distractor_logic: Molarity is temperature-dependent (volume changes on heating), so it is not used here.
Solvent mole fraction is the basis of relative vapour pressure lowering, not directly this formula.
Volume alone is not the variable in the ΔT<sub>b</sub> = K<sub>b</sub>m relation.

questions.question: Boiling point elevation is classified as a colligative property. This means K<sub>b</sub> for a given solvent, at a fixed molality, is:
options: The same regardless of which non-electrolyte solute is dissolved
Dependent on the solute's molar mass only, not its identity
Different for every different non-electrolyte solute
questions.explanation: Because ΔT<sub>b</sub> is colligative, it depends only on the number of solute particles (molality), not the chemical nature of the solute -- so for a fixed solvent, K<sub>b</sub> is a single constant that applies to any non-volatile, non-dissociating solute at that molality.
questions.hint: Colligative behaviour means the identity of the solute should not matter, only its particle count.
distractor_logic: K<sub>b</sub> does not depend on solute molar mass either -- it's a solvent property only.
Colour has no bearing on colligative properties.
This contradicts the colligative nature of the property; K<sub>b</sub> is solvent-specific, not solute-specific.

questions.question: Depression of freezing point (ΔT<sub>f</sub>) occurs because the solution's vapour pressure, being lower than that of the pure solvent, matches the vapour pressure of the solid solvent at a:
options: Temperature independent of the solvent's vapour pressure
Higher temperature than the pure solvent's freezing point
Temperature exactly equal to the pure solvent's freezing point
Lower temperature than the pure solvent's freezing point
questions.explanation: Freezing occurs when the vapour pressures of the liquid and solid phases become equal. Since dissolving a solute lowers the liquid's vapour pressure curve, this equality with the solid curve is reached at a lower temperature than for the pure solvent -- hence freezing point depression.
questions.hint: Freezing point is where the liquid and solid vapour-pressure curves intersect.
distractor_logic: The entire phenomenon arises specifically from the change in the liquid's vapour pressure.
It is a lower, not higher, temperature that satisfies the new equality.
If it were the same temperature there would be no depression at all.

questions.question: In ΔT<sub>f</sub> = K<sub>f</sub>m, K<sub>f</sub> is called the:
questions.explanation: K<sub>f</sub>, the molal depression constant (cryoscopic constant), is the freezing point depression caused by a 1 molal solution of a non-volatile non-electrolyte in a given solvent; like K<sub>b</sub>, it is a solvent property with units K kg mol<sup>−1</sup>.
questions.hint: It is defined 'per molal', hence the name molal depression constant.
distractor_logic: The van't Hoff factor i is a separate dissociation/association correction, not K<sub>f</sub> itself.
'Molar' concerns molarity, but K<sub>f</sub> is defined per unit molality, not molarity.
Ebullioscopic constant is the name for K<sub>b</sub> (boiling elevation), not K<sub>f</sub>.

questions.question: Ethylene glycol is added to water in car radiators mainly because it:
options: Increases the freezing point of water, preventing freezing damage
Increases the density of water only
Depresses the freezing point of water, preventing the coolant from freezing
Removes dissolved oxygen from the water
questions.explanation: Ethylene glycol is a non-volatile solute that, as a colligative effect, lowers the freezing point of the water-based coolant well below 0°C, preventing the radiator from freezing and cracking in cold climates -- a standard NCERT real-life application.
questions.hint: Antifreeze works by depressing, not raising, the freezing point.
distractor_logic: This is the opposite effect; dissolving a solute always lowers, never raises, the freezing point.
Density change is incidental, not the reason ethylene glycol is used as antifreeze.
Deoxygenation is not the purpose of antifreeze; the effect exploited is colligative freezing-point depression.

questions.question: Spreading salt (NaCl or CaCl<sub>2</sub>) on icy roads in winter helps clear ice because the salt:
options: Dissolves in the surface water film and depresses its freezing point below the ambient temperature
Increases the boiling point of water on the road
Has no effect on freezing point but simply provides grip
Chemically reacts with ice to produce heat
questions.explanation: Salt dissolves in the thin water film on ice, and the resulting depression of freezing point (ΔT<sub>f</sub> = iK<sub>f</sub>m, larger for NaCl/CaCl<sub>2</sub> due to dissociation) can push the freezing point below the outdoor temperature, so the ice melts and does not easily refreeze.
questions.hint: This uses the same freezing-point-depression principle as antifreeze, but for ionic solutes on roads.
distractor_logic: Boiling point elevation is irrelevant to melting ice at low ambient temperature.
The salt's effect is chemical/colligative (freezing point depression), not merely physical grip.
No significant exothermic chemical reaction between salt and ice drives this effect.

questions.question: Osmosis is the spontaneous flow of solvent molecules through a semipermeable membrane from:
options: A region of higher solute concentration to an equally concentrated region
A region of lower solute concentration (or pure solvent) to higher solute concentration
Any region to any other region, regardless of concentration
A region of higher solute concentration to lower solute concentration
questions.explanation: In osmosis, solvent moves from the side with lower solute concentration (higher solvent chemical potential) to the side with higher solute concentration (lower solvent chemical potential), through a membrane permeable only to the solvent, until osmotic equilibrium or until opposed by applied pressure.
questions.hint: Solvent moves toward the more concentrated solution, diluting it.
distractor_logic: Net osmotic flow requires a concentration difference; equal concentrations give no net flow.
Osmotic flow has a definite thermodynamic direction, set by the concentration gradient.
This reverses the actual direction of solvent flow in ordinary osmosis.

questions.question: Osmotic pressure (π) of a solution is defined as the excess pressure that must be applied to the solution side to:
options: Exactly stop net solvent flow through the membrane (osmotic equilibrium)
Reverse osmosis and push solvent into the pure-solvent side
questions.explanation: Osmotic pressure is the minimum excess pressure applied to the solution that just balances the tendency of solvent to flow in by osmosis, bringing the net solvent flow to zero -- i.e. establishing osmotic equilibrium across the membrane.
questions.hint: It's defined as the pressure that 'just stops' osmosis, not one that reverses or speeds it.
distractor_logic: Boiling point elevation is a separate colligative property, unrelated to this definition.
Applying pressure beyond π (not merely equal to it) is what causes reverse osmosis.
The pressure defining π opposes and halts osmosis, it does not accelerate it.

questions.question: The van't Hoff equation for osmotic pressure of a dilute solution, π = CRT, is analogous in form to:
options: The ideal gas equation, PV = nRT
questions.explanation: Van't Hoff noted that πV = nRT has exactly the same form as the ideal gas equation PV = nRT, with osmotic pressure π playing the role of pressure -- this analogy is a standard NCERT point (though the underlying physical origin is different).
questions.hint: Rearranged, πV = nRT looks structurally identical to one very famous gas-law equation.
distractor_logic: Hess's law is a thermochemistry law about enthalpy of reaction, unrelated here.
Raoult's law concerns vapour pressure of solutions, a different relationship.
Henry's law concerns gas solubility in liquids, not osmotic pressure.

questions.question: Two solutions having the same osmotic pressure at a given temperature are called:
questions.explanation: Solutions with equal osmotic pressure are termed isotonic; when placed on either side of a semipermeable membrane, no net osmosis occurs between them because their solvent escaping tendencies are equal (e.g. 0.9% saline is isotonic with blood plasma).
questions.hint: The prefix 'iso-' means 'equal', matching 'equal osmotic pressure'.

questions.question: In reverse osmosis, used for desalination of seawater, pressure applied on the solution side must be:
options: Greater than the osmotic pressure of seawater
Less than the osmotic pressure of seawater
Exactly equal to the osmotic pressure of seawater
Irrelevant; only membrane pore size matters
questions.explanation: Reverse osmosis forces pure solvent (water) to flow against its natural osmotic direction, from the concentrated (seawater) side to the dilute side. This requires applying pressure on the seawater side that exceeds its osmotic pressure, reversing the normal flow.
questions.hint: To reverse the natural direction of osmosis you must overcome it, not just match it.

Pressure exactly equal to π only achieves equilibrium (no net flow), not reversal.
Applied pressure relative to π is exactly what determines flow direction; pore size alone is not sufficient.

questions.topic: Abnormal Molar Mass and van't Hoff Factor
questions.question: The van't Hoff factor, i, is defined as the ratio:
options: Observed colligative property ÷ normal (calculated) colligative property
Normal colligative property ÷ observed colligative property
questions.explanation: i = (observed colligative property)/(calculated colligative property assuming no dissociation/association) = (normal molar mass)/(observed molar mass). For dissociating solutes i > 1; for associating solutes i < 1; for non-electrolytes i = 1.
questions.hint: It measures how much the actual behaviour deviates from the 'ideal, no dissociation' expectation.

questions.topic: Abnormal Molar Mass and van't Hoff Factor
questions.question: For a solute that dissociates into ions in solution (e.g. NaCl → Na<sup>+</sup> + Cl<sup>−</sup>), the van't Hoff factor i is expected to be:
questions.explanation: Dissociation increases the actual number of solute particles beyond what the formula mass suggests, so observed colligative properties are larger than the 'normal' calculated value, giving i > 1 (approaching i = 2 for full dissociation of NaCl into 2 ions).
questions.hint: More particles from dissociation should boost the observed colligative effect above normal.

questions.topic: Abnormal Molar Mass and van't Hoff Factor
questions.question: For a solute that associates (dimerises) in solution, such as acetic acid in benzene, the van't Hoff factor i is expected to be:
questions.explanation: Association reduces the effective number of independent solute particles (e.g. two acetic acid molecules combine into one dimer via H-bonding in benzene), so the observed colligative property is smaller than the 'normal' calculated value, giving i < 1 (approaching i = 0.5 for complete dimerisation).
questions.hint: Fewer independent particles than expected means the observed effect is weaker than normal.

i is perfectly well-defined for association; it is simply less than 1, not undefined.

questions.topic: Types of Solutions and Concentration Terms
questions.question: 10 g of a salt is dissolved in 90 g of water. What is the mass percentage of the salt in the solution?
questions.explanation: Mass % = (mass of solute / mass of solution) × 100 = (10 / (10 + 90)) × 100 = (10/100) × 100 = 10%.
questions.hint: Total mass of solution = mass of solute + mass of solvent.

This uses solvent mass (90 g) in the denominator instead of total solution mass (100 g).

questions.question: A solution contains 2 mol of glucose dissolved in 8 mol of water. What is the mole fraction of glucose?
questions.explanation: x<sub>glucose</sub> = n<sub>glucose</sub> / (n<sub>glucose</sub> + n<sub>water</sub>) = 2 / (2 + 8) = 2/10 = 0.2.

questions.explanation: Molarity M = moles of solute / volume of solution in litres = 0.5 mol / 0.250 L = 2 mol L<sup>−1</sup> = 2 M.

questions.explanation: ppm = (mass of solute / mass of solution) × 10<sup>6</sup>. Mass of solution = 1 kg = 1 × 10<sup>6</sup> mg. ppm = (2 mg / 1 × 10<sup>6</sup> mg) × 10<sup>6</sup> = 2.

It is weaker than the pure-component interactions
There is no intermolecular interaction between phenol and aniline
It is stronger than the pure-component interactions
