questions.question: 12 g of glucose (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>, molar mass 180 g mol<sup>−1</sup>) is dissolved in 500 g of water (K<sub>f</sub> = 1.86 K kg mol<sup>−1</sup>). What is the approximate depression in freezing point?
questions.explanation: Moles of glucose = 12/180 ≈ 0.0667 mol. Molality = 0.0667/0.5 = 0.1333 mol kg<sup>−1</sup>. ΔT<sub>f</sub> = 1.86 × 0.1333 ≈ 0.25 K.
questions.hint: Convert grams to moles, then moles to molality using the solvent's mass in kg, then apply ΔT<sub>f</sub> = K<sub>f</sub>m.
distractor_logic: 0.12 K is roughly half the correctly computed value.
0.93 K corresponds to a molality of exactly 0.5, not the molality found from these masses (0.133).
0.44 K is roughly double the correctly computed value.

questions.question: 2 g of a non-volatile solute dissolved in 100 g of water depresses the freezing point by 0.372 K (K<sub>f</sub> = 1.86 K kg mol<sup>−1</sup>). What is the molar mass of the solute?
questions.explanation: Molality m = ΔT<sub>f</sub>/K<sub>f</sub> = 0.372/1.86 = 0.2 mol kg<sup>−1</sup>. Moles of solute = 0.2 × 0.1 kg = 0.02 mol. Molar mass = 2/0.02 = 100 g mol<sup>−1</sup>.
questions.hint: Find molality from ΔT<sub>f</sub>, convert to moles using the (small) solvent mass in kg, then divide the given mass by moles.
distractor_logic: 25 g mol<sup>−1</sup> would follow from a moles value of 0.08 mol rather than the correct 0.02 mol.
50 g mol<sup>−1</sup> would follow from a moles value of 0.04 mol rather than the correct 0.02 mol.
200 g mol<sup>−1</sup> would follow from halving the correctly-computed moles value.

questions.question: A 0.2 molal solution of a non-volatile, non-electrolyte solute is prepared in benzene, for which K<sub>f</sub> = 5.12 K kg mol<sup>−1</sup>. What is the depression in freezing point?
questions.explanation: ΔT<sub>f</sub> = K<sub>f</sub>m = 5.12 × 0.2 = 1.024 K.
questions.hint: Multiply the given K<sub>f</sub> for benzene directly by the molality.
distractor_logic: 10.24 K is 10 times too large, from a decimal-point slip.
2.56 K does not correspond to correctly multiplying 5.12 by 0.2.
0.512 K is roughly half the correct value, as if the molality were 0.1 instead of 0.2.

questions.question: A solution has molarity 0.1 mol L<sup>−1</sup> at 300 K. Using π = CRT with R = 0.0821 L atm K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>, what is its osmotic pressure? (nearest 0.01 atm)
questions.explanation: π = CRT = 0.1 × 0.0821 × 300 = 2.463 ≈ 2.46 atm.
questions.hint: Multiply all three quantities together in one step.
distractor_logic: 24.6 atm is 10 times too large, from a decimal-point slip.
0.821 atm omits the factor of 300 (temperature) from the multiplication.
30 atm mistakenly omits R from the calculation, using only C × T.

questions.question: A solution has an osmotic pressure of 1.5 atm at 300 K. Using π = CRT with R = 0.0821 L atm K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>, what is its molar concentration? (nearest 0.01 mol L<sup>−1</sup>)
questions.hint: Rearrange π = CRT to C = π/(RT), computing the denominator RT first.
distractor_logic: 0.12 mol L<sup>−1</sup> is roughly double the correctly computed value.
0.03 mol L<sup>−1</sup> is roughly half the correctly computed value.
6.09 mol L<sup>−1</sup> results from forgetting to divide by RT at all, i.e. treating π × RT as the answer.

questions.question: 0.01 mol of a non-volatile solute is dissolved to make 250 mL of solution at 300 K. Using π = CRT with R = 0.0821 L atm K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>, what is the osmotic pressure of the solution? (nearest 0.01 atm)
questions.explanation: C = n/V = 0.01/0.25 = 0.04 mol L<sup>−1</sup>. π = CRT = 0.04 × 0.0821 × 300 ≈ 0.985 ≈ 0.99 atm.
questions.hint: First find molarity by dividing moles by the volume in litres (250 mL = 0.25 L), then apply π = CRT.
distractor_logic: 0.25 atm is simply the volume in litres, not the osmotic pressure at all.
9.85 atm is 10 times too large, from a decimal-point slip.
2.46 atm corresponds to a concentration of 0.1 mol L<sup>−1</sup>, not the correct 0.04 mol L<sup>−1</sup>.

questions.question: What amount (in moles) of a non-volatile solute must be dissolved in exactly 1 L of solution at 300 K to produce an osmotic pressure of 2.46 atm? (R = 0.0821 L atm K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>)
questions.explanation: C = π/(RT) = 2.46/(0.0821 × 300) = 2.46/24.63 ≈ 0.1 mol L<sup>−1</sup>. Since the volume is exactly 1 L, moles = C × V = 0.1 × 1 = 0.1 mol.
questions.hint: First find the required molarity from π = CRT, then multiply by the (here, conveniently 1 L) volume.
distractor_logic: 0.01 mol is 10 times too small compared to the correctly computed 0.1 mol.
1.0 mol is 10 times too large compared to the correctly computed 0.1 mol.
0.001 mol is 100 times too small compared to the correctly computed 0.1 mol.

questions.question: Solution A (0.05 mol L<sup>−1</sup>) at 300 K has osmotic pressure π<sub>A</sub>. Solution B, at 320 K, is found to have the same osmotic pressure π<sub>A</sub>. Using R = 0.0821 L atm K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>, are A and B isotonic, and what is the approximate molarity of B?
options: Isotonic (by definition of equal π), and C<sub>B</sub> ≈ 0.047 mol L<sup>−1</sup>
Not isotonic, since only equal molarity makes solutions isotonic
Isotonic (by definition of equal π), and C<sub>B</sub> ≈ 0.05 mol L<sup>−1</sup> exactly, since isotonic solutions must have equal molarity
Cannot be isotonic since they are at different temperatures
questions.explanation: π<sub>A</sub> = 0.05 × 0.0821 × 300 = 1.2315 atm. Since π<sub>B</sub> = π<sub>A</sub> by construction, the solutions ARE isotonic by definition (equal osmotic pressure). C<sub>B</sub> = π<sub>A</sub>/(RT<sub>B</sub>) = 1.2315/(0.0821 × 320) ≈ 1.2315/26.27 ≈ 0.047 mol L<sup>−1</sup>, which is close to but not exactly equal to C<sub>A</sub> because the temperatures differ.
questions.hint: Isotonic is defined purely by equal osmotic pressure, not by equal molarity or equal temperature.
distractor_logic: Isotonic is defined by equal osmotic pressure, regardless of whether molarities also happen to match.
Because T differs between A and B, equal π does NOT require equal molarity here -- C<sub>B</sub> works out to about 0.047, not exactly 0.05.
Osmotic pressure can be matched across different temperatures by adjusting concentration; equal π is the only requirement for 'isotonic', not equal temperature.

questions.topic: Abnormal Molar Mass and van't Hoff Factor
questions.question: A solute that fully dissociates into a maximum of 2 particles (like NaCl into Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup>) shows an experimental van't Hoff factor of i = 1.8. What is the degree of dissociation, α?
questions.explanation: For dissociation into n particles, i = 1 + (n − 1)α. Here n = 2, so 1.8 = 1 + (2 − 1)α = 1 + α, giving α = 0.8, i.e. 80% dissociation.
questions.hint: Use i = 1 + (n − 1)α with n = 2, so the equation simplifies to i = 1 + α.
distractor_logic: 1.0 (complete dissociation) would give i = 2.0 exactly, not the given i = 1.8.
0.5 would correspond to i = 1.5, not the given i = 1.8.
0.2 would correspond to i = 1.2, not the given i = 1.8.

questions.topic: Abnormal Molar Mass and van't Hoff Factor
questions.question: Acetic acid has a normal molar mass of 60 g mol<sup>−1</sup>. When dissolved in benzene, colligative property measurements give an abnormally high observed molar mass of 120 g mol<sup>−1</sup>, consistent with dimer formation. What is the van't Hoff factor i for acetic acid in benzene?
questions.explanation: i = normal molar mass / observed molar mass = 60/120 = 0.5, consistent with complete dimerisation (two acetic acid molecules associating into one dimer via hydrogen bonding), which is why i approaches 0.5 rather than 1.
questions.hint: Recall i = (normal molar mass)/(observed molar mass) for association cases.
distractor_logic: i = 1.5 does not correspond to the ratio 60/120.
i = 1.0 would apply to a non-associating, non-dissociating solute -- but here a doubled observed molar mass signals association.
i = 2.0 would apply to a solute that dissociates into 2 particles, the opposite of the association seen here.

questions.topic: Abnormal Molar Mass and van't Hoff Factor
questions.question: A 0.1 molal aqueous solution of an electrolyte has a van't Hoff factor i = 2.5 due to partial dissociation. Given K<sub>f</sub> for water = 1.86 K kg mol<sup>−1</sup>, what is the observed depression in freezing point, ΔT<sub>f</sub> = iK<sub>f</sub>m?
questions.explanation: ΔT<sub>f</sub> = iK<sub>f</sub>m = 2.5 × 1.86 × 0.1 = 0.465 K.
questions.hint: Multiply all three factors together: van't Hoff factor, K<sub>f</sub>, and molality.
distractor_logic: 0.186 K omits the van't Hoff factor i entirely (it is just K<sub>f</sub> × m / 10).
0.93 K corresponds to i = 5, not the given i = 2.5.
4.65 K is 10 times too large, from a decimal-point slip.

questions.topic: Types of Solutions and Concentration Terms
questions.question: A 20% (w/w) aqueous solution of KI (molar mass 166 g mol<sup>−1</sup>) has a density of 1.202 g mL<sup>−1</sup>. What are its molarity and molality (nearest 0.01)?
questions.explanation: Take 100 g of solution: 20 g KI (0.1205 mol) and 80 g water. Molality = 0.1205 mol / 0.080 kg = 1.51 mol kg<sup>−1</sup>. Volume of solution = 100 g / 1.202 g mL<sup>−1</sup> = 83.19 mL = 0.08319 L. Molarity = 0.1205 / 0.08319 = 1.45 mol L<sup>−1</sup>.
questions.hint: Work from a 100 g basis: find moles of KI, then divide by solvent mass (kg) for molality and by solution volume (L, via density) for molarity.
distractor_logic: This swaps the two computed values -- molarity and molality are interchanged.
Molarity of 2.00 M does not follow from correctly dividing moles of KI by the solution volume found via density.
1.20 simply reuses the density value as if it were the answer, without doing the mole/volume calculation.

questions.topic: Types of Solutions and Concentration Terms
questions.question: A 1 M aqueous NaOH solution (molar mass 40 g mol<sup>−1</sup>) has a density of 1.04 g mL<sup>−1</sup>. What is its molality?
questions.explanation: Take 1 L of solution: mass of solution = 1000 mL × 1.04 g mL<sup>−1</sup> = 1040 g. It contains 1 mol NaOH = 40 g. Mass of water = 1040 − 40 = 1000 g = 1 kg. Molality = 1 mol / 1 kg = 1.00 mol kg<sup>−1</sup>.
questions.hint: Convert the 1 L basis to total solution mass using density, subtract the solute's mass to get the solvent's mass, then divide.
distractor_logic: 1.04 mol kg<sup>−1</sup> just reuses the density value directly, without the subtraction step.
0.96 mol kg<sup>−1</sup> would follow from mistakenly using 1040 g (the whole solution) as the solvent mass instead of subtracting the solute.
1.08 mol kg<sup>−1</sup> does not follow from the correct mass-balance calculation shown.

questions.topic: Types of Solutions and Concentration Terms
questions.question: Dissolved oxygen in a river is reported as 5.8 ppm (by mass). Taking the solution's density as approximately 1 g mL<sup>−1</sup> and O<sub>2</sub>'s molar mass as 32 g mol<sup>−1</sup>, what is the approximate molar concentration of dissolved O<sub>2</sub>?
questions.explanation: 5.8 ppm means 5.8 g O<sub>2</sub> per 10<sup>6</sup> g solution. For 1 L of solution (≈ 1000 g at density 1 g mL<sup>−1</sup>), mass of O<sub>2</sub> = 1000 × 5.8/10<sup>6</sup> = 5.8 × 10<sup>−3</sup> g. Moles of O<sub>2</sub> = 5.8 × 10<sup>−3</sup>/32 ≈ 1.8 × 10<sup>−4</sup> mol, so molarity ≈ 1.8 × 10<sup>−4</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup>.
questions.hint: Chain the conversion: ppm → mass of O<sub>2</sub> per litre of solution → moles of O<sub>2</sub> → molarity.
distractor_logic: 1.8 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> is off by a factor of 10 from correctly dividing by 32.
5.8 × 10<sup>−4</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> skips dividing by the molar mass of O<sub>2</sub> (32).
5.8 × 10<sup>−6</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> is simply the ppm value reinterpreted as a mass fraction, without the mass-to-moles conversion.

questions.topic: Solubility of Gases in Liquids (Henry's Law)
questions.question: For O<sub>2</sub> dissolved in water at 298 K, K<sub>H</sub> = 3.30 × 10<sup>7</sup> mmHg. Air is roughly 20% O<sub>2</sub> by partial pressure, and atmospheric pressure is 760 mmHg. Approximately what mass of O<sub>2</sub> dissolves per litre of water in equilibrium with air? (Take 1 L water ≈ 55.5 mol.)
questions.explanation: p<sub>O2</sub> = 0.20 × 760 = 152 mmHg. x<sub>O2</sub> = p/K<sub>H</sub> = 152/(3.30 × 10<sup>7</sup>) ≈ 4.61 × 10<sup>−6</sup>. For dilute solution, n<sub>O2</sub> ≈ x<sub>O2</sub> × n<sub>water</sub> = 4.61 × 10<sup>−6</sup> × 55.5 ≈ 2.56 × 10<sup>−4</sup> mol. Mass = 2.56 × 10<sup>−4</sup> × 32 ≈ 8.2 × 10<sup>−3</sup> g = 8.2 mg.
questions.hint: Chain four steps: find p<sub>O2</sub>, then x<sub>O2</sub> from Henry's law, then moles of O<sub>2</sub> using the given moles of water, then convert to mass.
distractor_logic: 82 mg is 10 times too large compared to the correct chained calculation.
820 mg is 100 times too large and not physically reasonable for gas solubility at this pressure.
0.82 mg is 10 times too small compared to the correct chained calculation.

questions.topic: Solubility of Gases in Liquids (Henry's Law)
questions.question: A sealed 300 mL bottle of soda (approximate solvent mass 300 g) is bottled such that the partial pressure of CO<sub>2</sub> above the liquid is 3 atm. If K<sub>H</sub> for CO<sub>2</sub> in water under these conditions is 1250 atm, approximately what mass of CO<sub>2</sub> is dissolved in the bottle? (Take molar mass of water as 18 g mol<sup>−1</sup> and of CO<sub>2</sub> as 44 g mol<sup>−1</sup>.)
questions.explanation: x<sub>CO2</sub> = p/K<sub>H</sub> = 3/1250 = 0.0024. Moles of water = 300/18 ≈ 16.67 mol. Moles of CO<sub>2</sub> ≈ x<sub>CO2</sub> × n<sub>water</sub> = 0.0024 × 16.67 ≈ 0.04 mol. Mass of CO<sub>2</sub> = 0.04 × 44 = 1.76 g.
questions.hint: Chain: find x<sub>CO2</sub> from Henry's law, use it with moles of water to get moles of CO<sub>2</sub>, then convert to mass.
distractor_logic: 0.76 g does not correspond to correctly chaining all four steps shown.
0.176 g is 10 times too small compared to the correctly chained calculation.
17.6 g is 10 times too large compared to the correctly chained calculation.

questions.topic: Solubility of Gases in Liquids (Henry's Law)
questions.question: Two gases A and B are both in contact with the same solvent at a partial pressure of 10 atm each. K<sub>H</sub> for gas A is 1 × 10<sup>4</sup> atm and for gas B is 2 × 10<sup>4</sup> atm. Which gas is more soluble in the solvent, and by what factor?
options: Gas A is more soluble, by a factor of 2
Gas B is more soluble, by a factor of 2
Gas A is more soluble, by a factor of 4
questions.explanation: x<sub>A</sub> = p/K<sub>H,A</sub> = 10/(1 × 10<sup>4</sup>) = 1 × 10<sup>−3</sup>. x<sub>B</sub> = 10/(2 × 10<sup>4</sup>) = 5 × 10<sup>−4</sup>. Since x<sub>A</sub>/x<sub>B</sub> = 2, gas A (the one with the smaller K<sub>H</sub>) is twice as soluble as gas B at the same partial pressure.
questions.hint: Compute x = p/K<sub>H</sub> for each gas separately, then compare -- remember smaller K<sub>H</sub> means higher solubility.
distractor_logic: This reverses the relationship; the gas with the SMALLER K<sub>H</sub> (A) is more soluble, not the one with larger K<sub>H</sub>.
The correct ratio x<sub>A</sub>/x<sub>B</sub> works out to 2, not 4.
The two K<sub>H</sub> values differ by a factor of 2, so the solubilities cannot be equal.

questions.topic: Vapour Pressure of Solutions and Raoult's Law
questions.question: An ideal solution of benzene (p° = 150 mmHg) and toluene (p° = 50 mmHg) has a liquid-phase mole fraction of benzene x<sub>benzene</sub> = 0.3. What is the mole fraction of benzene in the vapour phase?
questions.explanation: p<sub>benzene</sub> = 0.3 × 150 = 45 mmHg. p<sub>toluene</sub> = 0.7 × 50 = 35 mmHg. p<sub>total</sub> = 45 + 35 = 80 mmHg. y<sub>benzene</sub> = p<sub>benzene</sub>/p<sub>total</sub> = 45/80 = 0.5625.
questions.hint: Find both partial pressures first, sum them for the total, then take the ratio for benzene's vapour-phase mole fraction.
distractor_logic: 0.4375 does not correspond to correctly dividing 45 by the correct total of 80.
0.30 is simply the liquid-phase mole fraction x<sub>benzene</sub>, not the vapour-phase y<sub>benzene</sub>.
0.75 does not follow from the correct partial-pressure calculation with these p° values.

questions.topic: Vapour Pressure of Solutions and Raoult's Law
questions.question: For an ideal solution of A (p<sub>A</sub>° = 200 mmHg) and B (p<sub>B</sub>° = 400 mmHg), the vapour phase is found to have y<sub>A</sub> = 0.4. What is the mole fraction of A in the liquid, x<sub>A</sub>?
questions.explanation: p<sub>A</sub> = 200x<sub>A</sub>, p<sub>B</sub> = 400(1 − x<sub>A</sub>). Since y<sub>A</sub> = p<sub>A</sub>/(p<sub>A</sub>+p<sub>B</sub>) = 0.4, we get p<sub>B</sub> = 1.5p<sub>A</sub>. Substituting: 400(1 − x<sub>A</sub>) = 1.5 × 200x<sub>A</sub> = 300x<sub>A</sub>, so 400 − 400x<sub>A</sub> = 300x<sub>A</sub>, giving x<sub>A</sub> = 400/700 ≈ 0.57.
questions.hint: Set up p<sub>B</sub> = 1.5p<sub>A</sub> from the vapour ratio, then substitute the Raoult's-law expressions and solve the resulting linear equation for x<sub>A</sub>.
distractor_logic: 0.43 does not follow from correctly solving 400(1−x<sub>A</sub>) = 300x<sub>A</sub>.
0.40 is simply the given vapour-phase value y<sub>A</sub>, not the liquid-phase x<sub>A</sub> being solved for.
0.60 (= 1 − 0.4) mistakenly treats y<sub>A</sub>'s complement as if it were x<sub>A</sub>.

questions.topic: Vapour Pressure of Solutions and Raoult's Law
questions.question: 39 g of benzene (molar mass 78 g mol<sup>−1</sup>, p° = 150 mmHg) is mixed with 46 g of toluene (molar mass 92 g mol<sup>−1</sup>, p° = 50 mmHg), forming an ideal solution. What is the total vapour pressure of this solution?
questions.explanation: Moles benzene = 39/78 = 0.5; moles toluene = 46/92 = 0.5, so x<sub>benzene</sub> = x<sub>toluene</sub> = 0.5 (equimolar mixture). p<sub>total</sub> = (0.5 × 150) + (0.5 × 50) = 75 + 25 = 100 mmHg.
questions.hint: First convert both masses to moles to find the actual mole fractions, then apply Raoult's law to each component.
distractor_logic: 150 mmHg is simply benzene's pure vapour pressure, unadjusted for the mixture's actual composition.
75 mmHg is only the partial pressure contributed by benzene, not the total vapour pressure.
125 mmHg does not follow from correctly weighting p° values by the (equal) mole fractions found here.

questions.question: A binary liquid mixture is observed to boil at a temperature lower than the boiling point of either pure component, at one specific composition; simple distillation cannot separate the mixture beyond that composition. What does this indicate about the mixture?
options: It shows negative deviation from Raoult's law and forms a maximum-boiling azeotrope
It is an ideal solution obeying Raoult's law exactly
It shows negative deviation and can always be fully separated by further distillation
It shows positive deviation from Raoult's law and forms a minimum-boiling azeotrope
questions.explanation: A boiling point lower than both pure components implies a vapour pressure maximum at that composition, which is the hallmark of strong positive deviation from Raoult's law; this vapour-pressure maximum (boiling-point minimum) is precisely a minimum-boiling azeotrope, at which the vapour and liquid have identical composition, making further separation by ordinary distillation impossible.
questions.hint: Link the boiling-point-minimum observation to a vapour-pressure maximum, and connect that to the type of deviation.
distractor_logic: Negative deviation produces maximum-boiling azeotropes (boiling higher, not lower, than either pure component).
An ideal solution's boiling point varies smoothly and monotonically between the two pure boiling points, with no minimum and no azeotrope.
Negative deviation is the wrong type here, and azeotropes (of either kind) specifically resist further separation by simple distillation.

questions.question: In a dilute non-ideal binary solution, as the mole fraction of the minor component (solute) x<sub>2</sub> → 0, its partial vapour pressure is found to follow p<sub>2</sub> = K<sub>H</sub>x<sub>2</sub> with K<sub>H</sub> ≠ p<sub>2</sub>°, while the major component (solvent) still follows Raoult's law. What does this illustrate?
options: Henry's law only applies to solutions of gases, never to liquid solutes
This behaviour is only possible in ideal solutions
Both components obey the same limiting law at all concentrations
The solvent obeys Raoult's law as x<sub>1</sub> → 1, while the dilute solute obeys Henry's law as x<sub>2</sub> → 0, reflecting the different environments each type of molecule experiences
questions.explanation: This is a general limiting-law result for real (non-ideal) dilute solutions: the solvent (present in large excess, x<sub>1</sub> → 1) is surrounded mostly by like molecules and behaves nearly ideally (Raoult's law), while the solute (present in trace amount, x<sub>2</sub> → 0) is surrounded almost entirely by solvent molecules in a different environment, so its escaping tendency is described by its own proportionality constant K<sub>H</sub> (Henry's law) rather than its own pure vapour pressure p<sub>2</sub>°.
questions.hint: Think about which component is 'surrounded by its own kind' (obeys Raoult's law) versus 'surrounded by the other kind' (obeys Henry's law) in a very dilute solution.
distractor_logic: Henry's law in this generalized form applies to any dilute solute, not only dissolved gases -- the given scenario is explicitly a liquid solution.

This solvent/solute limiting behaviour is a feature of real (non-ideal) solutions; an ideal solution obeys Raoult's law for both components at every composition, with no separate K<sub>H</sub> needed.
The two components follow different limiting laws precisely because their local molecular environments differ at x→0 versus x→1.

questions.question: An ideal solution is prepared from equal moles of A (p<sub>A</sub>° = 300 mmHg) and B (p<sub>B</sub>° = 100 mmHg). What is the mole fraction of A in the vapour, and is the vapour richer or poorer in A relative to the liquid?
options: y<sub>A</sub> = 0.25; vapour is poorer in A than the liquid
y<sub>A</sub> = 0.75; vapour is poorer in A than the liquid
y<sub>A</sub> = 0.75; vapour is richer in A than the liquid
y<sub>A</sub> = 0.50; vapour has the same composition as the liquid
questions.explanation: x<sub>A</sub> = x<sub>B</sub> = 0.5 (equimolar). p<sub>A</sub> = 0.5 × 300 = 150 mmHg; p<sub>B</sub> = 0.5 × 100 = 50 mmHg; p<sub>total</sub> = 200 mmHg. y<sub>A</sub> = 150/200 = 0.75, which is greater than the liquid's x<sub>A</sub> = 0.5 -- so the vapour is enriched (richer) in A, the more volatile component (higher p°).
questions.hint: Compute y<sub>A</sub> numerically first, then compare it directly to the given liquid-phase x<sub>A</sub> = 0.5.
distractor_logic: 0.25 does not follow from correctly weighting the partial pressures; also A (the more volatile component) should enrich, not deplete, the vapour.
The numeric value 0.75 is correct, but A being the more volatile component (higher p°) means the vapour is richer, not poorer, in A.
y<sub>A</sub> is not equal to x<sub>A</sub> here since A and B have very different p° values (300 vs 100 mmHg), so the vapour and liquid compositions differ.

questions.question: 18 g of glucose (molar mass 180 g mol<sup>−1</sup>) is dissolved in 90 g of water (molar mass 18 g mol<sup>−1</sup>, vapour pressure 25 mmHg at this temperature). Using the exact mole-fraction relation (not the dilute approximation), what is the vapour pressure of the resulting solution? (nearest 0.1 mmHg)
questions.explanation: Moles glucose = 18/180 = 0.1 mol; moles water = 90/18 = 5 mol. x<sub>2</sub> (glucose) = 0.1/(5 + 0.1) = 0.0196. p = p°(1 − x<sub>2</sub>) = 25 × (1 − 0.0196) = 25 × 0.9804 ≈ 24.51 mmHg.
questions.hint: Compute moles of both components exactly, find x<sub>2</sub> using the exact denominator (n<sub>1</sub> + n<sub>2</sub>), then apply p = p°(1 − x<sub>2</sub>).
distractor_logic: 25.00 mmHg ignores the solute's effect entirely, treating the vapour pressure as unchanged.
23.75 mmHg would follow from using x<sub>2</sub> = 0.05, not the correctly computed 0.0196.
24.90 mmHg would follow from using x<sub>2</sub> ≈ 0.004, an underestimate of the correct value.

questions.question: 5 g of a non-volatile solute (molar mass 60 g mol<sup>−1</sup>) is dissolved in an unknown mass of benzene (molar mass 78 g mol<sup>−1</sup>), producing a relative lowering of vapour pressure of 0.05. Using the dilute approximation n<sub>2</sub>/n<sub>1</sub> ≈ x<sub>2</sub>, what mass of benzene was used?
questions.explanation: Moles of solute n<sub>2</sub> = 5/60 ≈ 0.0833 mol. Since x<sub>2</sub> ≈ n<sub>2</sub>/n<sub>1</sub> = 0.05, n<sub>1</sub> = n<sub>2</sub>/0.05 = 0.0833/0.05 ≈ 1.667 mol. Mass of benzene = 1.667 × 78 ≈ 130 g.
questions.hint: First find moles of solute, then use the dilute relative-lowering relation to back out moles of solvent, then convert to mass using benzene's molar mass.
distractor_logic: 65 g would follow from n<sub>1</sub> ≈ 0.833 mol, half the correctly computed value.
78 g is simply benzene's molar mass reused directly, not the actual mass of benzene present.
104 g does not follow from correctly dividing n<sub>2</sub> by 0.05 and multiplying by 78.

questions.question: A solvent A (4 mol) has two different non-volatile solutes dissolved in it simultaneously: 0.05 mol of B and 0.03 mol of C. What is the relative lowering of vapour pressure of A? (Treat both solutes together as contributing to the total solute mole fraction.)
questions.explanation: Total moles of solute = 0.05 + 0.03 = 0.08 mol. Total moles overall = 4 + 0.08 = 4.08 mol. x<sub>solute, total</sub> = 0.08/4.08 ≈ 0.0196, which equals the relative lowering of vapour pressure of A (Raoult-Ostwald law extends naturally to multiple non-volatile solutes by summing their moles).
questions.hint: Combine the moles of both solutes into a single total solute mole count before dividing by the total moles present.
distractor_logic: 0.0075 does not correspond to any correct combination of the given mole amounts.
0.08 is simply the total moles of solute, not divided by the total moles of the mixture.
0.0125 does not correspond to a correct application of the total-mole-fraction relation.

questions.question: 10 g of a non-volatile solute (molar mass 40 g mol<sup>−1</sup>) is dissolved in 200 g of an unknown solvent, giving a relative lowering of vapour pressure of 0.045. Using the approximation (p<sub>1</sub>°−p<sub>1</sub>)/p<sub>1</sub>° ≈ (w<sub>2</sub>/M<sub>2</sub>)/(w<sub>1</sub>/M<sub>1</sub>), what is the molar mass of the solvent, M<sub>1</sub>?
questions.hint: Rearrange the approximate formula to isolate M<sub>1</sub> on one side, substituting the known w<sub>2</sub>, M<sub>2</sub>, and w<sub>1</sub> values.
distractor_logic: 72 g mol<sup>−1</sup> is double the correctly computed value, from a factor-of-2 slip.
18 g mol<sup>−1</sup> (water's molar mass) does not follow from solving this particular equation for M<sub>1</sub>.
58 g mol<sup>−1</sup> does not follow from the correct algebraic rearrangement shown.

questions.question: A solute (normal molar mass 120 g mol<sup>−1</sup>) is 80% associated into dimers in benzene (K<sub>b</sub> = 2.53 K kg mol<sup>−1</sup>). For a 0.2 molal solution, what is the observed elevation in boiling point?
questions.explanation: For association into n = 2 units with degree of association α = 0.8: i = 1 − (1 − 1/n)α = 1 − (1 − 0.5)(0.8) = 1 − 0.4 = 0.6. ΔT<sub>b</sub> = iK<sub>b</sub>m = 0.6 × 2.53 × 0.2 ≈ 0.304 K.
questions.hint: First find i using the association formula i = 1 − (1 − 1/n)α with n = 2, then multiply by K<sub>b</sub>m as usual.
distractor_logic: 0.506 K is the elevation assuming i = 1 (no association at all), which contradicts the given 80% association.
0.405 K does not follow from correctly computing i = 0.6 and multiplying by K<sub>b</sub>m.
0.253 K is the elevation for a 0.1 molal solution with i = 1, ignoring both the given molality and the association.

questions.question: A 0.1 molal aqueous solution of a weak monoprotic acid HA (which dissociates as HA → H<sup>+</sup> + A<sup>−</sup>) is found to be 4% dissociated. Given K<sub>b</sub> for water = 0.52 K kg mol<sup>−1</sup>, what is the boiling point elevation of this solution?
questions.explanation: For dissociation into n = 2 particles with degree of dissociation α = 0.04: i = 1 + (n − 1)α = 1 + (1)(0.04) = 1.04. ΔT<sub>b</sub> = iK<sub>b</sub>m = 1.04 × 0.52 × 0.1 ≈ 0.054 K.
questions.hint: First compute i = 1 + (n − 1)α with n = 2 for this weak acid, then apply ΔT<sub>b</sub> = iK<sub>b</sub>m.
distractor_logic: 0.104 K is roughly double the correctly computed value.
0.052 K assumes i = 1 (no dissociation at all), ignoring the given 4% dissociation.
0.541 K would require a much larger i (around 10.4), far more than the modest 4% dissociation given.

questions.question: A 0.05 molal aqueous solution of an electrolyte AB (which can dissociate into 2 ions) shows an experimental boiling point elevation of 0.052 K (K<sub>b</sub> = 0.52 K kg mol<sup>−1</sup>). What is the degree of dissociation of AB in this solution?
questions.explanation: ΔT<sub>b</sub> calculated assuming no dissociation (i = 1) = K<sub>b</sub>m = 0.52 × 0.05 = 0.026 K. i = observed/calculated = 0.052/0.026 = 2.0. For n = 2, i = 1 + α so α = i − 1 = 1.0, i.e. 100% dissociation.
questions.hint: First find the 'no dissociation' baseline ΔT<sub>b</sub> using i = 1, then compare to the observed value to get i, then extract α.
distractor_logic: 50% dissociation would give i = 1.5 and ΔT<sub>b</sub> = 0.039 K, not the observed 0.052 K.
80% dissociation would give i = 1.8 and ΔT<sub>b</sub> = 0.0468 K, not the observed 0.052 K.
92% dissociation would give i = 1.92, close to but not matching the exact i = 2.0 required by the data.

questions.question: A student computes that a certain solute, dissociating into n = 2 ions, should give ΔT<sub>b</sub> = 0.30 K if fully dissociated in a 0.2887 molal aqueous solution (K<sub>b</sub> = 0.52 K kg mol<sup>−1</sup>). The actual experimental value comes out lower, at 0.18 K. What does this indicate?
options: The solute is only partially dissociated (i between 1 and 2), consistent with a weak electrolyte
K<sub>b</sub> for water must be different from 0.52 K kg mol<sup>−1</sup> in this case
The solute is dissociating more than 100%, which is impossible, so the data must be wrong
The solute must be undergoing association instead of dissociation
questions.explanation: The 'fully dissociated' value assumes i = 2 (n = 2, α = 1). Since the observed ΔT<sub>b</sub> (0.18 K) is lower than this full-dissociation prediction (0.30 K) but still higher than the i = 1 (no dissociation) value of 0.15 K, the actual i lies between 1 and 2 -- exactly the signature of a weak electrolyte that dissociates only partially rather than completely.
questions.hint: Compare the observed value to both the i = 1 (no dissociation) and i = 2 (full dissociation) extremes to see where it falls.
distractor_logic: K<sub>b</sub> is a solvent property (fixed for water); the discrepancy is explained by incomplete dissociation, not by K<sub>b</sub> changing.
i above 2 is not implied here; the observed value is actually lower than the full-dissociation prediction, not higher.
Association would push i below 1 (below the no-dissociation baseline of 0.15 K), but 0.18 K is above that baseline, ruling out association.

questions.question: Benzoic acid (normal molar mass 122 g mol<sup>−1</sup>) is found to dimerise essentially completely (100% association) in benzene via hydrogen bonding. What is the abnormal (observed) molar mass of benzoic acid measured via freezing point depression in benzene?
questions.explanation: For complete dimerisation, n = 2, α = 1: i = 1 − (1 − 1/2)(1) = 1 − 0.5 = 0.5. Observed molar mass = normal molar mass / i = 122/0.5 = 244 g mol<sup>−1</sup>.
questions.hint: Find i for complete dimerisation first (it approaches 0.5), then divide the normal molar mass by i.
distractor_logic: 61 g mol<sup>−1</sup> is half the normal molar mass, the reciprocal of the correct relationship (dividing instead of the correct division direction).
122 g mol<sup>−1</sup> is simply the normal (undissociated, unassociated) molar mass, ignoring the dimerisation entirely.
183 g mol<sup>−1</sup> does not follow from correctly dividing 122 by i = 0.5.

questions.question: A 0.1 molal aqueous solution of KCl gives an experimental freezing point depression of 0.352 K (K<sub>f</sub> = 1.86 K kg mol<sup>−1</sup>). What is the percentage dissociation of KCl in this solution?
questions.explanation: i = ΔT<sub>f</sub>/(K<sub>f</sub>m) = 0.352/(1.86 × 0.1) = 0.352/0.186 ≈ 1.892. For KCl dissociating into n = 2 ions: α = i − 1 ≈ 0.892, i.e. about 89.2% dissociation.
questions.hint: Compute i first by dividing the observed ΔT<sub>f</sub> by the 'no dissociation' value K<sub>f</sub>m, then extract α = i − 1 for n = 2.
distractor_logic: 82.5% does not correspond to the i value obtained from these exact numbers.
78.3% does not correspond to the i value obtained by correctly dividing 0.352 by 0.186.
94.6% would require i ≈ 1.946, slightly higher than the actual i ≈ 1.892 computed from the data.

questions.question: MgCl<sub>2</sub>, which fully dissociates into 3 ions (Mg<sup>2+</sup> + 2Cl<sup>−</sup>) in the ideal case, is dissolved to make a 0.05 molal aqueous solution (K<sub>f</sub> = 1.86 K kg mol<sup>−1</sup>). The observed freezing point depression is 0.25 K, somewhat less than the fully-dissociated prediction. What is the approximate percentage dissociation actually occurring?
questions.explanation: The 'no dissociation' baseline is K<sub>f</sub>m = 1.86 × 0.05 = 0.093 K. Observed i = 0.25/0.093 ≈ 2.688. For n = 3, α = (i − 1)/(n − 1) = (2.688 − 1)/2 = 1.688/2 ≈ 0.844, i.e. about 84%.
questions.hint: Find i by comparing the observed ΔT<sub>f</sub> to the i = 1 baseline, then use α = (i − 1)/(n − 1) with n = 3 for this triatomic-ion electrolyte.
distractor_logic: 56% does not correspond to the i value obtained by correctly dividing 0.25 by 0.093.
78% is close to but not exactly the value obtained from the precise division and n = 3 formula.
67% would follow from mistakenly using n = 2 instead of the correct n = 3 for MgCl<sub>2</sub>.

questions.question: 34.2 g of sucrose (C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>22</sub>O<sub>11</sub>, molar mass 342 g mol<sup>−1</sup>, a non-electrolyte) is dissolved in 500 g of water (K<sub>f</sub> = 1.86 K kg mol<sup>−1</sup>, normal freezing point 0°C). What is the freezing point of this solution?
questions.explanation: Moles of sucrose = 34.2/342 = 0.1 mol. Molality = 0.1/0.5 = 0.2 mol kg<sup>−1</sup>. ΔT<sub>f</sub> = K<sub>f</sub>m = 1.86 × 0.2 = 0.372 K. Freezing point = 0°C − 0.372 K = −0.372°C.
questions.hint: Convert mass to moles, then to molality using the solvent mass in kg, then apply ΔT<sub>f</sub> = K<sub>f</sub>m and subtract from 0°C.
distractor_logic: −1.86°C corresponds to a molality of exactly 1, not the molality found from these masses (0.2).
−0.744°C corresponds to a molality of 0.4, double the correctly computed value.
−0.186°C corresponds to a molality of 0.1, half the correctly computed 0.2 mol kg<sup>−1</sup>.

questions.question: Blood plasma at body temperature (310 K) has an osmotic pressure of about 7.65 atm. Assuming NaCl (which dissociates completely, i = 2) is used to prepare an isotonic saline solution, what molar concentration of NaCl is required? (R = 0.0821 L atm K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>)
questions.explanation: Using π = iCRT: C = π/(iRT) = 7.65/(2 × 0.0821 × 310) = 7.65/50.90 ≈ 0.15 mol L<sup>−1</sup>.
questions.hint: Include the van't Hoff factor i = 2 in the denominator since NaCl fully dissociates into two ions.
distractor_logic: 0.30 mol L<sup>−1</sup> is exactly double the correct value, as if i had been omitted (used as 1) after halving some other way.
1.50 mol L<sup>−1</sup> is 10 times too large, from a decimal-point slip in the division.
0.075 mol L<sup>−1</sup> is exactly half the correct value, as if i had been mistakenly used as 4 instead of 2.

questions.question: Seawater has an osmotic pressure of approximately 25 atm at a certain temperature. A reverse osmosis desalination plant applies 30 atm of pressure to the seawater side of a semipermeable membrane. What is the net effective pressure actually driving pure water to flow from the seawater side to the fresh water side?
options: 5 atm, driving flow toward the fresh water side (reverse osmosis occurring)
55 atm, in the reverse osmosis direction
25 atm, in the normal osmosis direction
5 atm, driving flow toward the seawater side (normal osmosis still dominates)
questions.explanation: Reverse osmosis requires applied pressure to exceed the solution's own osmotic pressure. Here, applied pressure (30 atm) exceeds π (25 atm) by 30 − 25 = 5 atm, so there is a net 5 atm pressure forcing pure water to flow from the concentrated seawater side to the dilute (fresh water) side -- the reverse of the natural osmotic direction.
questions.hint: Subtract the seawater's own osmotic pressure from the externally applied pressure to find the net driving pressure.
distractor_logic: 55 atm mistakenly adds the two pressures rather than taking their difference.
25 atm is simply π itself, not the net pressure after subtracting it from the applied 30 atm.
Since applied pressure exceeds π, the net flow is in the reverse-osmosis direction (toward fresh water), not back toward the seawater side.

questions.question: 1 g of a protein is dissolved to make 200 mL of solution. At 300 K, the osmotic pressure of this solution is measured as 2.57 × 10<sup>−3</sup> atm (R = 0.0821 L atm K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>). What is the approximate molar mass of the protein?
questions.explanation: C = π/(RT) = 2.57 × 10<sup>−3</sup>/(0.0821 × 300) ≈ 1.04 × 10<sup>−4</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup>. Moles in 200 mL = 1.04 × 10<sup>−4</sup> × 0.2 ≈ 2.09 × 10<sup>−5</sup> mol. Molar mass = 1 g / 2.09 × 10<sup>−5</sup> mol ≈ 4.79 × 10<sup>4</sup> g mol<sup>−1</sup>. (This large value, and the need for a very sensitive method like osmotic pressure, is typical for macromolecules such as proteins.)
questions.hint: Chain: find molar concentration from π = CRT, convert to moles using the actual 200 mL volume, then divide the given mass by moles.
distractor_logic: 4.79 × 10<sup>3</sup> g mol<sup>−1</sup> is 10 times too small compared to the fully chained calculation.
2.09 × 10<sup>2</sup> g mol<sup>−1</sup> is simply the moles-in-200-mL figure misread as the final molar mass.
4.79 × 10<sup>5</sup> g mol<sup>−1</sup> is 10 times too large compared to the fully chained calculation.

questions.question: Two solutions, P and Q, both have the same osmotic pressure at the same temperature (i.e. they are isotonic, with equal effective particle concentration). If equal volumes of P and Q are mixed, what is the osmotic pressure of the resulting mixture, compared to the original solutions?
options: It cannot be predicted without knowing the identity of the solutes
It remains the same as the original osmotic pressure
It doubles, since the total number of solute particles has doubled
It halves, since the volume has doubled but particle number has not
questions.explanation: Osmotic pressure depends only on the particle concentration (moles of effective particles per litre), not on total particle number or total volume alone. Since P and Q are isotonic, they have equal particle concentration; mixing equal volumes doubles both the total particles AND the total volume proportionally, leaving the concentration -- and hence the osmotic pressure -- unchanged.
questions.hint: Focus on concentration (particles per litre), not on total particle count or total volume in isolation.
distractor_logic: Because osmotic pressure is colligative (depends only on effective particle concentration, not solute identity), the outcome can be predicted without knowing what P and Q actually contain.
This confuses total particle count with concentration; osmotic pressure depends on concentration, which is unchanged by mixing equal-concentration solutions.
Volume alone does not determine osmotic pressure; since particle number scales up in the same proportion as volume, concentration -- and π -- stays constant.

questions.topic: Abnormal Molar Mass and van't Hoff Factor
questions.question: A solute of normal molar mass 180 g mol<sup>−1</sup> undergoes association in a certain solvent such that 60% of the solute molecules combine into trimers (3 molecules → 1 aggregate), the rest remaining unassociated. What is the apparent (observed) molar mass of the solute in this solvent?
questions.explanation: For association into n = 3 units with degree of association α = 0.6: i = 1 − (1 − 1/3)α = 1 − (2/3)(0.6) = 1 − 0.4 = 0.6. Observed molar mass = normal molar mass/i = 180/0.6 = 300 g mol<sup>−1</sup>.
questions.hint: Use i = 1 − (1 − 1/n)α with n = 3 (trimerisation), then divide the normal molar mass by i.
distractor_logic: 150 g mol<sup>−1</sup> does not follow from correctly dividing 180 by the computed i = 0.6.
540 g mol<sup>−1</sup> would follow from using i = 1/3 directly, without accounting for the 60% (partial) association.
108 g mol<sup>−1</sup> would follow from multiplying (rather than dividing) the normal molar mass by i = 0.6.

questions.topic: Abnormal Molar Mass and van't Hoff Factor
questions.question: A complex salt is expected to dissociate completely into a maximum of 4 ions in aqueous solution. Colligative property measurements give an experimental van't Hoff factor of i = 3.4. What is the degree of dissociation of the salt?
questions.explanation: For n = 4 (maximum possible ions): i = 1 + (n − 1)α = 1 + 3α. Solving 3.4 = 1 + 3α gives α = 2.4/3 = 0.8, i.e. 80% dissociation.
questions.hint: Use i = 1 + (n − 1)α with n = 4, and solve for α directly.
distractor_logic: 68% does not correspond to correctly solving 3.4 = 1 + 3α.
85% would correspond to i = 3.55, not the given i = 3.4.
75% would correspond to i = 3.25, not the given i = 3.4.

questions.question: For an aqueous solution of a given molality, K<sub>f</sub> = 1.86 K kg mol<sup>−1</sup> and K<sub>b</sub> = 0.52 K kg mol<sup>−1</sup>. Approximately how many times larger is the freezing point depression than the boiling point elevation, for the same solution?
questions.explanation: Since both ΔT<sub>f</sub> = K<sub>f</sub>m and ΔT<sub>b</sub> = K<sub>b</sub>m use the same molality m, their ratio is simply K<sub>f</sub>/K<sub>b</sub> = 1.86/0.52 ≈ 3.58, so ΔT<sub>f</sub> is roughly 3.6 times ΔT<sub>b</sub> for water at any given molality.
questions.hint: The molality cancels in the ratio ΔT<sub>f</sub>/ΔT<sub>b</sub>, leaving just K<sub>f</sub>/K<sub>b</sub>.
distractor_logic: 2.6 does not match the ratio 1.86/0.52.
5.2 does not match the ratio 1.86/0.52 (this looks like K<sub>b</sub> × 10, not the actual ratio).
1.5 does not match the ratio 1.86/0.52.

questions.question: For measuring the molar mass of a macromolecule like a protein present only in trace amounts, osmotic pressure measurements are generally preferred over boiling point elevation measurements. What is the main reason?
options: Boiling point elevation only works for volatile solutes
Even at very low solute concentration, osmotic pressure produces a comparatively large, easily measurable value, while ΔT<sub>b</sub> would be too tiny to measure accurately
Osmotic pressure does not depend on the amount of solute present
Osmotic pressure measurements do not require knowing the temperature
questions.explanation: Because π = CRT involves the large factor RT (about 24.6 L atm mol<sup>−1</sup> at 300 K), even a very dilute solution (as is necessary for large, sparingly soluble macromolecules) gives a measurable osmotic pressure, whereas the corresponding ΔT<sub>b</sub> = K<sub>b</sub>m would be far too small (a small fraction of a kelvin) to measure precisely with ordinary equipment.
questions.hint: Compare the practical size of π versus ΔT<sub>b</sub> for the very small concentrations typical of macromolecule solutions.
distractor_logic: Boiling point elevation works for any non-volatile solute, dissolved or macromolecular; volatility of the solute is not the deciding factor here.
Osmotic pressure is itself proportional to solute concentration -- it very much depends on the amount present, just as ΔT<sub>b</sub> does.
Osmotic pressure measurements still require T (it appears explicitly in π = CRT); this is not the reason for the preference.

questions.question: A 0.05 molal aqueous solution of an electrolyte shows an experimental freezing point depression of 0.20 K (K<sub>f</sub> = 1.86 K kg mol<sup>−1</sup>). Assuming the same van't Hoff factor applies, what osmotic pressure would this solution (taken as 0.05 M) show at 300 K? (R = 0.0821 L atm K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>)
questions.explanation: From ΔT<sub>f</sub>: i = 0.20/(1.86 × 0.05) = 0.20/0.093 ≈ 2.15. Using the same i in π = iCRT: π = 2.15 × 0.05 × 0.0821 × 300 ≈ 2.65 atm.
questions.hint: First extract i from the freezing point data, then carry that same i over into the osmotic pressure formula.
distractor_logic: 1.23 atm corresponds to i = 1 (no dissociation at all), ignoring the freezing point data.
3.10 atm would require i ≈ 2.52, higher than the i ≈ 2.15 obtained from the given freezing point data.
1.85 atm does not follow from correctly carrying i ≈ 2.15 into π = iCRT.
mixed_topics: Abnormal Molar Mass and van't Hoff Factor

questions.topic: Solubility of Gases in Liquids (Henry's Law)
questions.question: Air is approximately 21% O<sub>2</sub> by partial pressure, and total atmospheric pressure is 760 mmHg. For O<sub>2</sub> in water, K<sub>H</sub> = 3.30 × 10<sup>7</sup> mmHg. Taking 1 L of water as 55.5 mol, what is the approximate molar concentration of dissolved O<sub>2</sub> at equilibrium with air?
questions.explanation: p<sub>O2</sub> = 0.21 × 760 = 159.6 mmHg. x<sub>O2</sub> = 159.6/(3.30 × 10<sup>7</sup>) ≈ 4.84 × 10<sup>−6</sup>. Moles O<sub>2</sub> per litre ≈ x<sub>O2</sub> × 55.5 ≈ 2.68 × 10<sup>−4</sup> mol, so molarity ≈ 2.68 × 10<sup>−4</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup>.
questions.hint: Chain: find p<sub>O2</sub>, then x<sub>O2</sub> via Henry's law, then multiply by moles of water per litre to get molarity.
distractor_logic: 4.84 × 10<sup>−6</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> is simply x<sub>O2</sub> itself, not yet converted to molarity by multiplying by 55.5.
1.60 × 10<sup>−2</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> is far too large for a gas this poorly soluble at 1 atm-scale partial pressures.
2.68 × 10<sup>−6</sup> mol L<sup>−1</sup> is 100 times too small, from a decimal-point slip.
