questions.topic: Vapour Pressure of Solutions and Raoult's Law
questions.question: The relative lowering of vapour pressure relation (p<sub>1</sub>° − p<sub>1</sub>)/p<sub>1</sub>° = x<sub>2</sub> is used to determine a dissolved solute's molar mass. Would this exact relation remain valid if the 'solute' were itself volatile (e.g. determining the molar mass of dissolved ethanol in water)?
options: No -- the relation assumes the solute is non-volatile and contributes no vapour pressure of its own; a volatile solute also evaporates, so the simple relation no longer applies
No, because volatile solutes cannot form solutions with water at all
Yes, the relation holds for any solute regardless of volatility
Yes, but only if the solute's molar mass is less than the solvent's
questions.explanation: The Raoult-Ostwald relation is derived specifically under the assumption that only the solvent evaporates (p<sub>solute</sub> ≈ 0). If the solute is volatile, it contributes its own partial pressure, so the total vapour pressure must be found using Raoult's law for both components (p<sub>total</sub> = x<sub>1</sub>p<sub>1</sub>° + x<sub>2</sub>p<sub>2</sub>°), and the simple lowering-equals-x<sub>2</sub> shortcut breaks down.
questions.hint: Revisit the assumption baked into the derivation of (p<sub>1</sub>°−p<sub>1</sub>)/p<sub>1</sub>° = x<sub>2</sub> -- specifically, what it assumes about the solute's own vapour pressure.
distractor_logic: Ethanol and water do form solutions readily (indeed a classic example of positive deviation); the issue is the formula's assumption, not solubility.
The derivation explicitly assumes a non-volatile solute; it is not a general relation valid for any solute.
Relative molar mass has no bearing on whether the relation applies; volatility of the solute is what matters.
mixed_topics: Vapour Pressure of Solutions and Raoult's Law

questions.question: Equal masses of two different non-volatile, non-electrolyte solutes X and Y are separately dissolved in equal masses of the same solvent. Solute X produces a larger freezing point depression than solute Y. What can be concluded about their molar masses?
options: Y has a larger molar mass than X
X has a larger molar mass than Y
No conclusion about molar mass is possible
X and Y must have identical molar masses
questions.explanation: For a fixed mass of solute and solvent, ΔT<sub>f</sub> = K<sub>f</sub>m ∝ K<sub>f</sub>(mass/M<sub>solute</sub>), i.e. ΔT<sub>f</sub> is inversely proportional to the solute's molar mass. Since X shows the LARGER ΔT<sub>f</sub>, X must have the SMALLER molar mass (more moles per gram), meaning Y has the larger molar mass.
questions.hint: For the same mass dissolved, more moles (and hence a bigger colligative effect) means a smaller molar mass, not a larger one.
distractor_logic: This reverses the inverse relationship between ΔT<sub>f</sub> and molar mass for a fixed mass of solute.
The inverse relationship between ΔT<sub>f</sub> and molar mass (at fixed mass and solvent) is exactly what allows this comparison to be made.
Since their ΔT<sub>f</sub> values differ, their molar masses cannot be identical (for the same mass dissolved in the same solvent mass).
mixed_topics: Types of Solutions and Concentration Terms

questions.question: A binary liquid mixture forms a minimum-boiling azeotrope at 80 mole % component A. If a solution starting at 50 mole % A is subjected to repeated simple distillation, what is the eventual outcome?
options: The composition approaches the azeotropic composition (80% A), which then distils over unchanged, and complete separation into pure A and pure B is not achieved by simple distillation
Pure B distils off first, leaving pure A behind
The mixture separates completely into pure A and pure B after enough distillation cycles
Pure A distils off first, leaving pure B behind
questions.explanation: Repeated distillation of a mixture with a minimum-boiling azeotrope drives the residual liquid composition toward the azeotropic point; once reached, the vapour and liquid have identical composition (80% A), so the azeotrope distils over unchanged and simple distillation cannot separate it into the two pure components.
questions.hint: The defining feature of an azeotrope is that liquid and vapour compositions become identical there, so ordinary distillation stalls at that point.
distractor_logic: Neither pure component is obtained this way; the mixture stalls at the intermediate azeotropic composition instead.
Complete separation into pure components by simple distillation is exactly what an azeotrope prevents.
Neither pure component is obtained this way; the mixture stalls at the intermediate azeotropic composition instead.
mixed_topics: Vapour Pressure of Solutions and Raoult's Law

questions.question: For a given electrolyte dissolved in water at a fixed dilute concentration, the van't Hoff factor i is determined once from freezing point depression data, and separately once from osmotic pressure data. Assuming the solution is dilute enough to behave ideally in both measurements, what should be true of the two i values obtained?
options: i can only be measured using freezing point depression, not osmotic pressure
They will generally be different, since i is specific to each colligative property
They can only be compared if the temperature is the same for both measurements

They should agree closely, since i for a given solute-solvent pair at a given dilute concentration reflects the same underlying degree of dissociation/association, regardless of which colligative property is used to probe it
questions.explanation: The van't Hoff factor reflects a physical property of the solute in that solvent at that concentration -- how many effective particles are actually present per formula unit -- which does not depend on which colligative property happens to be used to detect it. For an ideally-behaving dilute solution, i extracted from ΔT<sub>f</sub>, ΔT<sub>b</sub>, relative lowering of vapour pressure, or π should all agree.
questions.hint: i describes the solute's actual dissociation/association behaviour, which is a single physical fact independent of the measurement method used to reveal it.
distractor_logic: i can be extracted from any of the four colligative properties, including osmotic pressure, as this very comparison illustrates.
This misunderstands what i represents; it is a property of the solute's behaviour in solution, not an artifact of the particular colligative property measured.
Temperature affects the size of each colligative property but not the fundamental value of i itself, which is about particle count, not temperature.
mixed_topics: Abnormal Molar Mass and van't Hoff Factor

questions.question: K<sub>b</sub> for water is 0.52 K kg mol<sup>−1</sup>, while K<sub>b</sub> for benzene is 2.53 K kg mol<sup>−1</sup>. For the same non-volatile, non-electrolyte solute dissolved at the same molality, in which solvent would you observe the larger boiling point elevation, and roughly how many times larger?
options: They would be identical, since ΔT<sub>b</sub> is colligative and solvent-independent
questions.explanation: Since ΔT<sub>b</sub> = K<sub>b</sub>m and m is the same in both cases, the ratio of elevations equals the ratio of K<sub>b</sub> values: 2.53/0.52 ≈ 4.9. Benzene, having the larger K<sub>b</sub>, shows the larger boiling point elevation for the same molality.
questions.hint: K<sub>b</sub> is a solvent-specific constant; a larger K<sub>b</sub> directly means a larger ΔT<sub>b</sub> for the same molality.
distractor_logic: 'Colligative' means independent of solute identity at a given concentration, not independent of the solvent -- K<sub>b</sub> itself is a solvent property and clearly differs between water and benzene.
This picks the wrong solvent; benzene, not water, has the larger K<sub>b</sub> and hence the larger elevation.
2.5 does not match the actual ratio 2.53/0.52 ≈ 4.9.
mixed_topics: Types of Solutions and Concentration Terms

questions.question: A dilute non-volatile solute is dissolved in water such that the relative lowering of vapour pressure is 0.02. Taking 1 kg of water as approximately 55.5 mol, what is the approximate molality of this solution? (Use the dilute approximation x<sub>2</sub> ≈ n<sub>2</sub>/n<sub>1</sub>.)
questions.explanation: x<sub>2</sub> ≈ n<sub>2</sub>/n<sub>1</sub>, so n<sub>2</sub> ≈ x<sub>2</sub> × n<sub>1</sub> = 0.02 × 55.5 ≈ 1.11 mol. Since n<sub>1</sub> here is exactly the moles in 1 kg of water, this n<sub>2</sub> value is directly the molality: ≈ 1.11 mol kg<sup>−1</sup>.
questions.hint: Multiply the relative lowering (≈ x<sub>2</sub>) directly by the moles of water in 1 kg.
distractor_logic: 2.78 mol kg<sup>−1</sup> is roughly 2.5 times too large compared to the correct calculation.
0.36 mol kg<sup>−1</sup> does not follow from correctly multiplying 0.02 by 55.5.
5.55 mol kg<sup>−1</sup> would follow from using x<sub>2</sub> = 0.1 instead of the given 0.02.
mixed_topics: Types of Solutions and Concentration Terms

questions.topic: Solubility of Gases in Liquids (Henry's Law)
questions.question: In a very dilute non-ideal binary solution, as the mole fraction of the minor component x<sub>2</sub> → 0, it is observed that p<sub>2</sub> = K<sub>H</sub>x<sub>2</sub>, while the major component simultaneously obeys p<sub>1</sub> = x<sub>1</sub>p<sub>1</sub>° as x<sub>1</sub> → 1. What best explains why the same solution can show two different limiting laws at once?
options: This can only happen if the solution is an ideal solution obeying Raoult's law exactly
Henry's law and Raoult's law are actually the same law written in different units
It cannot happen; only one law can apply to a solution at a time

The major component (solvent) is mostly surrounded by molecules of its own kind and behaves nearly as it would as a pure liquid (Raoult's law), while the minor component (solute) is almost entirely surrounded by unlike molecules and needs its own proportionality constant K<sub>H</sub> (Henry's law) to describe its escaping tendency
questions.explanation: In a dilute solution, the solvent molecules are overwhelmingly surrounded by other solvent molecules, so their environment (and hence escaping tendency) closely resembles the pure liquid -- Raoult's law. The solute molecules, being few, are essentially always surrounded by solvent, a completely different environment from their own pure liquid/gas state -- hence they follow their own empirical proportionality constant, K<sub>H</sub>, which need not equal p<sub>2</sub>°.
questions.hint: Compare the immediate molecular environment of a solvent molecule (surrounded by like molecules) versus a dilute solute molecule (surrounded by unlike molecules).
distractor_logic: This dual-law behaviour is a hallmark of real, non-ideal dilute solutions; a solution that is ideal throughout obeys Raoult's law for both components at every composition, with no separate K<sub>H</sub> needed.

They are conceptually related (both linear in mole fraction) but structurally distinct: Raoult's law ties its constant to the pure component's own p°, while Henry's law's K<sub>H</sub> is an independent empirical constant.
Both limiting laws can and do apply simultaneously, to different components, in the same dilute solution.
mixed_topics: Solubility of Gases in Liquids (Henry's Law)
Vapour Pressure of Solutions and Raoult's Law

questions.question: A solute that dissociates in solution (van't Hoff factor i > 1) is used to prepare a solution of a given molar concentration C. Compared to the osmotic pressure that would be calculated assuming no dissociation (π<sub>calc</sub> = CRT), the actual observed osmotic pressure π<sub>obs</sub> will be:
options: Zero, since dissociated ions do not contribute to osmotic pressure
questions.explanation: π<sub>obs</sub> = iπ<sub>calc</sub>. Since dissociation gives i > 1 (more effective particles than the formula suggests), π<sub>obs</sub> is necessarily greater than the π<sub>calc</sub> value computed assuming no dissociation.
questions.hint: Recall π<sub>obs</sub>/π<sub>calc</sub> = i, and that dissociation always makes i > 1.
distractor_logic: This would be true for association (i < 1), not dissociation.
Equality would only hold for a non-dissociating, non-associating solute (i = 1).
Dissociated ions are still solute particles and still contribute to (in fact enhance) osmotic pressure; they do not eliminate it.
mixed_topics: Abnormal Molar Mass and van't Hoff Factor

questions.question: An electrolyte and a non-electrolyte are each dissolved separately in water to make solutions of the same molality. The electrolyte dissociates partially (i > 1). Which solution shows the greater boiling point elevation?
options: Neither elevates the boiling point, since only freezing point is affected by dissolved solutes
Both show exactly the same elevation, since ΔT<sub>b</sub> is colligative and depends only on molality
questions.explanation: ΔT<sub>b</sub> = iK<sub>b</sub>m. The non-electrolyte has i = 1, while the electrolyte has i > 1 due to dissociation, so at the same molality m and same K<sub>b</sub>, the electrolyte solution produces the larger boiling point elevation.
questions.hint: The colligative property depends on the effective particle concentration (im), not just the formula-unit molality m.
distractor_logic: The non-electrolyte has the smaller i (exactly 1), so it gives the smaller, not larger, elevation.
Boiling point elevation, like freezing point depression, occurs for any solute (electrolyte or not) that lowers the solvent's vapour pressure -- both effects arise from the same underlying cause.
'Colligative' means depending on the number of particles, not on the formula-unit molality alone; dissociation changes the effective particle count, and hence ΔT<sub>b</sub>, via the factor i.
mixed_topics: Abnormal Molar Mass and van't Hoff Factor

questions.topic: Types of Solutions and Concentration Terms
questions.question: 5.85 g of NaCl (molar mass 58.5 g mol<sup>−1</sup>, which dissociates completely, i = 2) is dissolved to make 500 mL of solution at 300 K. Using π = iCRT with R = 0.0821 L atm K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>, what is the osmotic pressure of this solution?
questions.explanation: Moles NaCl = 5.85/58.5 = 0.1 mol. Molarity C = 0.1/0.5 = 0.2 mol L<sup>−1</sup>. π = iCRT = 2 × 0.2 × 0.0821 × 300 ≈ 9.85 atm.
questions.hint: Chain: find moles, then molarity (using the 500 mL volume), then apply π = iCRT with i = 2 for full NaCl dissociation.
distractor_logic: 4.93 atm corresponds to a concentration of 0.1 mol L<sup>−1</sup> (i.e. using the moles directly as if the volume were 1 L), not the correct 0.2 mol L<sup>−1</sup>.
2.46 atm uses i = 1, ignoring NaCl's dissociation into two ions entirely.
19.7 atm is double the correct value, as if i = 4 had been mistakenly used instead of i = 2.
mixed_topics: Types of Solutions and Concentration Terms
Abnormal Molar Mass and van't Hoff Factor

questions.topic: Vapour Pressure of Solutions and Raoult's Law
questions.question: A student tries to determine the molar mass of ethanol dissolved in water by measuring the relative lowering of vapour pressure and applying (p<sub>1</sub>°−p<sub>1</sub>)/p<sub>1</sub>° = n<sub>2</sub>/(n<sub>1</sub>+n<sub>2</sub>), treating ethanol as the 'solute'. Why would this experiment fail to give ethanol's correct (known) molar mass?
options: Because ethanol is completely insoluble in water
Because ethanol is itself volatile and contributes its own partial vapour pressure, violating the non-volatile-solute assumption behind this formula
Because water and ethanol form an ideal solution, and ideal solutions cannot be analysed by vapour pressure methods
Because the formula only works for solutes with molar mass greater than that of the solvent
questions.explanation: The relative-lowering formula assumes the measured drop in total vapour pressure is due entirely to the non-volatile solute occupying space at the surface, with the solute contributing essentially zero vapour pressure itself. Ethanol is volatile and evaporates alongside water (in fact ethanol-water shows positive deviation from Raoult's law), so the total vapour pressure reflects both components, and this simple formula cannot correctly isolate ethanol's molar mass.
questions.hint: Ask whether the 'solute' in this scenario truly contributes negligible vapour pressure of its own, which the formula requires.
distractor_logic: Ethanol is in fact fully miscible with water in all proportions; insolubility is not the issue.

Ideal solutions can still be analysed via Raoult's law using the full two-component treatment; the issue here is specifically the non-volatile-solute assumption of the relative-lowering shortcut, not ideality itself.
The formula's validity depends on the solute being non-volatile, not on any comparison of molar masses between solute and solvent.
mixed_topics: Vapour Pressure of Solutions and Raoult's Law

questions.question: The simple relation ΔT<sub>b</sub> = K<sub>b</sub>m is derived assuming dilute, essentially ideal solution behaviour. For a concentrated solution of a solute that causes strong positive deviation from Raoult's law, would you expect this simple linear relation to still hold accurately at high concentration?
options: No, because concentrated solutions never boil at all

No -- at high concentration with strong deviation from ideality, the actual boiling point elevation can deviate noticeably from the simple K<sub>b</sub>m prediction, which strictly assumes dilute, near-ideal behaviour
Yes, but only if the solute is ionic
Yes, ΔT<sub>b</sub> = K<sub>b</sub>m holds exactly at any concentration for any solute
questions.explanation: K<sub>b</sub> and the linear relation ΔT<sub>b</sub> = K<sub>b</sub>m are derived using approximations valid for dilute solutions (where Raoult's law nearly holds for the solvent). At higher concentrations, especially with a solute causing strong non-ideal (deviating) behaviour, these approximations break down and the observed ΔT<sub>b</sub> can differ from the simple prediction.
questions.hint: Recall that K<sub>b</sub> and its linear formula are dilute-solution approximations, not exact laws valid at all concentrations.
distractor_logic: Concentrated solutions still boil, just possibly not exactly at the temperature the simple dilute formula predicts.
The breakdown at high concentration is about deviation from ideal (Raoult's law) behaviour in general, not specifically about whether the solute is ionic.
The formula is a dilute-solution approximation, not an exact law valid at every concentration and for every degree of non-ideality.

questions.question: Both relative lowering of vapour pressure and boiling point elevation are colligative properties derived from the same underlying Raoult's law effect. In an ordinary school/college laboratory, which is generally easier to measure accurately, and why?
options: Boiling point elevation, because it can be measured with an ordinary precision thermometer, whereas accurately measuring small vapour pressure differences typically needs specialised manometric equipment
Relative lowering of vapour pressure, because it requires no thermometer at all
They are equally easy to measure by any standard laboratory method
Neither can be measured in an ordinary laboratory setting
questions.explanation: Boiling point elevation is detected as a temperature shift, measurable with a fairly ordinary (if sufficiently precise) thermometer. Measuring the small differences in vapour pressure directly, by contrast, typically requires more specialised manometric apparatus capable of resolving small pressure changes -- making ΔT<sub>b</sub> measurement more practically accessible.
questions.hint: Think about what physical quantity is directly read off in each method: a temperature change versus a small pressure difference.
distractor_logic: Vapour pressure lowering is measured via pressure-sensing apparatus, not by avoiding measurement altogether.
The two methods are not equally accessible; boiling point elevation is generally the more practically convenient of the two.
Boiling point elevation, in particular, is routinely measurable with standard laboratory thermometry.

questions.question: 6 g of urea (a non-volatile non-electrolyte, molar mass 60 g mol<sup>−1</sup>) is dissolved to make 1 L of solution. At 300 K (R = 0.0821 L atm K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>), the osmotic pressure is measured as 2.46 atm. Does this measured value correctly reproduce urea's known molar mass of 60 g mol<sup>−1</sup> when worked backward?
options: This cannot be checked without knowing urea's boiling point elevation as well
No -- working backward gives a molar mass of about 30 g mol<sup>−1</sup>, half the known value
Yes -- working backward from π = 2.46 atm gives C ≈ 0.1 mol L<sup>−1</sup>, hence M ≈ 6/0.1 = 60 g mol<sup>−1</sup>, matching the known value
No -- working backward gives a molar mass of about 120 g mol<sup>−1</sup>, double the known value
questions.explanation: C = π/(RT) = 2.46/(0.0821 × 300) ≈ 0.1 mol L<sup>−1</sup>. Moles present = C × V = 0.1 × 1 = 0.1 mol. Molar mass = mass/moles = 6/0.1 = 60 g mol<sup>−1</sup>, exactly matching urea's known molar mass -- confirming the internal consistency of the π = CRT relation for this non-electrolyte.
questions.hint: Reverse the π = CRT calculation step by step: find C, then moles, then divide the given mass by moles.
distractor_logic: This check can be done directly from the given osmotic pressure data alone; no additional boiling point data is required.
This would follow from an error that doubles the calculated moles (e.g. mistakenly using i = 2 for a non-electrolyte).
This would follow from an error that halves the calculated moles.
mixed_topics: Types of Solutions and Concentration Terms

questions.topic: Solubility of Gases in Liquids (Henry's Law)
questions.question: For a dilute gas dissolved in a liquid, the Henry's law constant K<sub>H</sub> is generally NOT equal to the gas's own vapour pressure as a pure liquid, p°<sub>gas</sub> (indeed, many gases have no well-defined 'pure liquid vapour pressure' at ordinary conditions at all). What does this reflect about the nature of K<sub>H</sub>?
options: K<sub>H</sub> can always be calculated theoretically from p°<sub>gas</sub> using a simple conversion factor
K<sub>H</sub> is simply a typographical alternative symbol for p°<sub>gas</sub>
This shows Henry's law is not really based on the same underlying idea as Raoult's law

K<sub>H</sub> is an independent, empirically determined proportionality constant reflecting how strongly the specific gas-solvent pair interact, and does not need to relate to any 'pure liquid' state of the gas at all
questions.explanation: Unlike Raoult's law (where the proportionality constant is explicitly the pure liquid's own p°), Henry's law's K<sub>H</sub> is a purely empirical constant specific to each gas-solvent pair and temperature; it need not correspond to any physical 'pure liquid vapour pressure' of the gas, since many gases (like O<sub>2</sub> or N<sub>2</sub>) do not even exist as ordinary liquids at the temperatures/pressures where the gas solubility is measured.
questions.hint: Consider that many common gases simply have no 'pure liquid vapour pressure' at room temperature and pressure at all.
distractor_logic: K<sub>H</sub> must be determined experimentally for each gas-solvent pair; there is no simple universal conversion from a (often non-existent) p°<sub>gas</sub>.
They play structurally analogous roles (as proportionality constants) but are not interchangeable symbols for the same physical quantity.
Henry's law and Raoult's law are conceptually related, both being limiting proportionality laws for the two extremes (dilute solute, x→0, vs near-pure solvent, x→1) of a real solution.
mixed_topics: Solubility of Gases in Liquids (Henry's Law)

questions.topic: Solubility of Gases in Liquids (Henry's Law)
questions.question: Henry's law describes gas solubility as an equilibrium in which gas molecules continuously leave and return between the gas phase above a liquid and the dissolved state. Boiling point elevation, by contrast, describes a non-volatile solute that never leaves the liquid phase at all. Why does this distinction matter for how the two phenomena are modelled?
options: Henry's law cannot be applied to any solution that also shows boiling point elevation

Henry's law inherently involves a genuine gas-liquid phase equilibrium with the dissolved species escaping and returning, while boiling point elevation is a colligative effect of a solute that stays put in solution and only indirectly affects the solvent's own escape into vapour
Boiling point elevation actually also requires the solute to partly vaporise, just like Henry's law
It doesn't matter -- both are described by exactly the same mathematical relation, K = p/x
questions.explanation: Henry's law is fundamentally about an equilibrium of the SOLUTE itself between dissolved and gaseous states (the solute is volatile as a gas by definition). Boiling point elevation, in contrast, concerns a solute that is non-volatile and remains entirely in solution -- what changes is only the SOLVENT's vapour pressure and hence its own boiling behaviour, not any escape of the solute.
questions.hint: Ask which species is doing the 'escaping into vapour' in each scenario -- the solute itself, or only the solvent.
distractor_logic: A solution can, in principle, show both a dissolved gas obeying Henry's law and a separate non-volatile solute causing boiling point elevation at the same time -- the two are not mutually exclusive.
By definition, the solute causing boiling point elevation is non-volatile and does not vaporise; if it did, the phenomenon would need a different (Raoult's-law, two-component) treatment altogether.
The two phenomena are governed by structurally different relations for different reasons (a genuine phase equilibrium for the solute vs. a colligative effect on the solvent).
mixed_topics: Solubility of Gases in Liquids (Henry's Law)

questions.question: A solute with normal molar mass 100 g mol<sup>−1</sup> associates partially in a solvent. A 0.2 molal solution shows an experimental freezing point depression of only 0.15 K (K<sub>f</sub> = 1.86 K kg mol<sup>−1</sup>). What is the apparent (observed) molar mass of the solute in this solvent?
questions.explanation: i = ΔT<sub>f</sub>/(K<sub>f</sub>m) = 0.15/(1.86 × 0.2) = 0.15/0.372 ≈ 0.403 (i < 1 confirms association). Observed molar mass = normal molar mass/i = 100/0.403 ≈ 248 g mol<sup>−1</sup>.
questions.hint: First find i by dividing the observed ΔT<sub>f</sub> by the 'no association' value K<sub>f</sub>m, then divide the normal molar mass by i.
distractor_logic: 40.3 g mol<sup>−1</sup> would follow from multiplying (rather than dividing) 100 by i ≈ 0.403.
186 g mol<sup>−1</sup> is simply K<sub>f</sub> × 100, an unrelated combination of numbers, not the correct division.
124 g mol<sup>−1</sup> does not follow from correctly dividing 100 by the computed i.
mixed_topics: Abnormal Molar Mass and van't Hoff Factor

questions.question: An electrolyte solute, if it behaved as a non-electrolyte at the given concentration, would give a mole fraction x<sub>2</sub> = 0.02 and hence a 'normal' relative lowering of 0.02. Because it actually dissociates with van't Hoff factor i = 1.8, what is the ACTUAL relative lowering of vapour pressure observed?
questions.explanation: Just as other colligative formulas are modified by i, the relative lowering formula becomes (p<sub>1</sub>°−p<sub>1</sub>)/p<sub>1</sub>° = ix<sub>2</sub> for a dissociating/associating solute. Actual relative lowering = i × x<sub>2</sub> = 1.8 × 0.02 = 0.036.
questions.hint: Multiply the 'normal' (non-electrolyte-equivalent) relative lowering by the van't Hoff factor i, just as with ΔT<sub>b</sub> = iK<sub>b</sub>m and ΔT<sub>f</sub> = iK<sub>f</sub>m.
distractor_logic: 0.020 is just the 'normal' value, without applying the van't Hoff correction for dissociation at all.
0.011 would follow from dividing rather than multiplying by i.
0.029 does not follow from correctly multiplying 0.02 by 1.8.
mixed_topics: Abnormal Molar Mass and van't Hoff Factor

questions.topic: Types of Solutions and Concentration Terms
questions.question: A solution is prepared by dissolving 23 g of ethanol (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH, molar mass 46 g mol<sup>−1</sup>, p° = 40 mmHg at this temperature) in 77 g of water. Treating this as an ideal solution obeying Raoult's law, what is the approximate partial vapour pressure contributed by ethanol? (Use the mole fraction of ethanol found earlier to be about 0.105.)
questions.explanation: By Raoult's law, p<sub>ethanol</sub> = x<sub>ethanol</sub> × p°<sub>ethanol</sub> = 0.105 × 40 ≈ 4.2 mmHg.
questions.hint: First find the mole fraction of ethanol (from the mass-percentage data), then multiply by its pure vapour pressure.
distractor_logic: 10.5 mmHg does not correspond to correctly multiplying 0.105 by 40.
23.0 mmHg is simply the mass of ethanol used (in grams), unrelated to the vapour pressure calculation.
0.42 mmHg is 10 times too small, from a decimal-point slip.
mixed_topics: Types of Solutions and Concentration Terms
Vapour Pressure of Solutions and Raoult's Law

questions.question: A student is asked to find the total vapour pressure of an ideal solution given the mass percentage composition of two volatile liquids and their pure vapour pressures. The student plugs the mass percentages directly into p<sub>total</sub> = x<sub>1</sub>p<sub>1</sub>° + x<sub>2</sub>p<sub>2</sub>° in place of x<sub>1</sub> and x<sub>2</sub>. What is wrong with this approach?
options: Raoult's law requires mole fractions specifically; mass percentages must first be converted to moles (using each component's molar mass) and then to mole fractions before use
Nothing -- mass percentage and mole fraction can always be used interchangeably in Raoult's law
The student's approach is correct only if both components have exactly equal molar masses
Raoult's law cannot be applied unless the composition is given in molarity
questions.explanation: x<sub>1</sub> and x<sub>2</sub> in Raoult's law are strictly mole fractions (moles of that component divided by total moles), not mass fractions. Using mass percentages directly is only coincidentally correct if the two components happen to have identical molar masses; in general, mass % must first be converted to moles via each component's own molar mass, and only then to mole fractions.
questions.hint: Check the definitions carefully: Raoult's law's x terms are mole-based, but mass percentage is a mass-based ratio.
distractor_logic: They are numerically different in general (unless molar masses happen to be equal), so this substitution is not generally valid.
This describes exactly the one special case where mass % and mole % coincide; in general (different molar masses) the direct substitution is wrong, which is the point being tested.
Raoult's law is defined directly in terms of mole fractions, which can be obtained from mass percentage after conversion -- molarity is not required at all.
mixed_topics: Types of Solutions and Concentration Terms

questions.question: Van't Hoff pointed out that πV = nRT has the same mathematical form as the ideal gas equation PV = nRT. Does this mean that the physical assumptions behind an 'ideal solution' (as used in Raoult's law) and an 'ideal gas' are the same thing?
options: Yes, they describe identical physical assumptions about the particles involved
Yes, because osmotic pressure is literally caused by gas molecules trapped in the solution

No -- the resemblance is a formal/mathematical analogy in the equations' structure; 'ideal solution' (Raoult's law, obeyed across the full concentration range with Δ<sub>mix</sub>H = Δ<sub>mix</sub>V = 0) and 'ideal gas' (non-interacting point particles) are conceptually distinct ideas that happen to give similarly-shaped equations
No, because the van't Hoff osmotic pressure equation does not actually involve the gas constant R
questions.explanation: The similarity between πV = nRT and PV = nRT is a well-known formal analogy (both are linear relations among a 'pressure-like' quantity, volume, moles, and temperature), but the physical pictures behind them differ: an ideal gas assumes negligible interactions between widely-spaced gas molecules, while an ideal solution (Raoult's law) is about vapour pressure behaviour of two liquids with equal A-A, A-B, and B-B interactions. Recognising the analogy is useful, but it should not be mistaken for physical identity.
questions.hint: Ask whether two equations having the same mathematical form necessarily means the underlying physics is identical.
distractor_logic: The physical situations (dissolved solute particles in a liquid vs. widely-separated gas molecules) are fundamentally different, even though the resulting equations look alike.
Osmotic pressure arises from solvent molecules crossing a semipermeable membrane due to a concentration difference, not from any literal population of gas molecules inside the solution.
R does appear explicitly in the van't Hoff equation π = CRT, which is exactly the basis for the analogy being discussed.

questions.question: For water, what molality of a non-volatile, non-electrolyte solute would be needed to produce a boiling point elevation of exactly 1 K (K<sub>b</sub> = 0.52 K kg mol<sup>−1</sup>), and what molar concentration would be needed to produce an osmotic pressure of exactly 1 atm at 300 K (R = 0.0821 L atm K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>)? Which target is reached with less solute?
options: Molality ≈ 1.92 mol kg<sup>−1</sup> for 1 K; molarity ≈ 0.041 mol L<sup>−1</sup> for 1 atm -- far less solute is needed to produce a comparably 'sized' osmotic pressure signal
Molality ≈ 1.92 mol kg<sup>−1</sup> for 1 K; molarity ≈ 24.6 mol L<sup>−1</sup> for 1 atm -- boiling point elevation needs far less solute
Molality ≈ 0.52 mol kg<sup>−1</sup> for 1 K; molarity ≈ 0.041 mol L<sup>−1</sup> for 1 atm -- boiling point elevation needs less solute
Both require exactly the same amount of solute, about 0.52 mol
questions.explanation: For ΔT<sub>b</sub> = 1 K: m = 1/K<sub>b</sub> = 1/0.52 ≈ 1.92 mol kg<sup>−1</sup>. For π = 1 atm: C = 1/(RT) = 1/(0.0821 × 300) ≈ 0.041 mol L<sup>−1</sup>. Far less solute (about 1/47th as much, roughly) is needed to reach a measurable-scale (1-unit) osmotic pressure signal than to reach a 1 K boiling point shift -- illustrating why osmotic pressure is the more sensitive method for dilute solutions.
questions.hint: Compute each required concentration separately by rearranging its respective formula, then compare the two numbers directly.
distractor_logic: 24.6 mol L<sup>−1</sup> would be RT itself, not the concentration obtained by dividing 1 by RT.
0.52 mol kg<sup>−1</sup> is simply K<sub>b</sub> itself, not the molality needed for exactly ΔT<sub>b</sub> = 1 K (which requires dividing 1 by K<sub>b</sub>).
The two required concentrations are not equal; the osmotic pressure route needs far less solute for a comparably 'sized' 1-unit signal.

questions.question: In the dilute limit, both relative lowering of vapour pressure ((p<sub>1</sub>°−p<sub>1</sub>)/p<sub>1</sub>° ≈ x<sub>2</sub>) and osmotic pressure (π = CRT) are directly proportional to the solute's concentration. If the solute concentration is doubled (while staying dilute), what happens to each of these two colligative properties?
options: Relative lowering doubles, but osmotic pressure stays the same
Osmotic pressure doubles, but relative lowering stays the same
questions.explanation: Because both relations are linear (first-order/direct proportionality) in solute concentration in the dilute regime, doubling the solute amount (at fixed solvent amount/volume) causes both the relative lowering of vapour pressure and the osmotic pressure to roughly double as well.
questions.hint: Both formulas are of the form (colligative property) = (constant) × (concentration) -- a direct proportionality.
distractor_logic: Osmotic pressure is exactly as directly proportional to concentration (via π = CRT) as relative lowering is to mole fraction; there is no reason for one to change and not the other.
Relative lowering is exactly as directly proportional to solute mole fraction as osmotic pressure is to concentration; both should respond, not just one.
Direct proportionality means the effect scales by the same factor as the cause (doubling gives doubling), not a squared (quadrupling) response.

questions.question: 0.4 mol of a non-volatile, non-electrolyte solute is dissolved in 2 kg of water (K<sub>b</sub> = 0.52 K kg mol<sup>−1</sup>, K<sub>f</sub> = 1.86 K kg mol<sup>−1</sup>, normal boiling point 100°C, normal freezing point 0°C). This uses double the correct molality (0.4 instead of 0.2 mol kg<sup>−1</sup>), perhaps from forgetting to divide by the 2 kg of solvent.
This swaps the two ΔT values -- boiling point elevation should use K<sub>b</sub> (giving the smaller shift), freezing point depression should use K<sub>f</sub> (giving the larger shift).

questions.topic: Solubility of Gases in Liquids (Henry's Law)
questions.question: Henry's law (p<sub>2</sub> = K<sub>H</sub>x<sub>2</sub>) and the Raoult-Ostwald relative lowering relation ((p<sub>1</sub>°−p<sub>1</sub>)/p<sub>1</sub>° = x<sub>2</sub>) are both linear relationships between a vapour-pressure-related quantity and a solution-phase mole fraction x<sub>2</sub>. What is the key structural difference between the two proportionality constants involved?
options: Henry's law's K<sub>H</sub> is always exactly double the Raoult's law constant

In the Raoult-Ostwald relation, the constant is explicitly the solvent's own pure vapour pressure p<sub>1</sub>°; in Henry's law, K<sub>H</sub> is an independent empirical constant for the dissolved gas, not necessarily tied to any 'pure' vapour pressure of that species
There is no difference; K<sub>H</sub> and p<sub>1</sub>° always have exactly the same numerical value
The Raoult-Ostwald relation's constant depends on temperature, but K<sub>H</sub> does not
questions.explanation: In the Raoult-Ostwald relation, the coefficient linking relative lowering to x<sub>2</sub> traces back directly to the solvent's own measurable pure vapour pressure p<sub>1</sub>°. Henry's law's K<sub>H</sub>, by contrast, is a separate empirically measured constant for each gas-solvent pair, which need not (and generally does not) equal any 'pure' vapour pressure value for the dissolved gas.
questions.hint: Compare where each constant 'comes from': one is literally the solvent's own known vapour pressure; the other is measured independently for each gas-solvent system.
distractor_logic: There is no fixed universal ratio of exactly 2 between the two; each is determined independently by its own physical/chemical system.
These are generally different quantities, measured under quite different physical contexts (a pure liquid's vapour pressure vs. an empirical gas-solubility constant).
Both K<sub>H</sub> and p<sub>1</sub>° are temperature-dependent quantities; temperature dependence is not the distinguishing feature here.

questions.question: The 'ideal solution' concept (Raoult's law obeyed exactly across the full composition range, Δ<sub>mix</sub>H = Δ<sub>mix</sub>V = 0) is usually illustrated with mixtures of two similar volatile liquids, like benzene and toluene. Colligative-property problems involving a van't Hoff factor (electrolyte dissociation, or solute association) are typically treated as:
options: Only applicable to gaseous solutions, not liquid ones

Dilute solutions of a (usually) non-volatile solute, analysed using the dilute-solution limiting laws -- these are a different (though related) scenario from the strict two-volatile-liquid 'ideal solution' definition, and the van't Hoff factor is simply layered on top of the usual dilute colligative-property formulas
Never related to vapour pressure or Raoult's law in any way
Ideal solutions in exactly this strict Raoult's-law sense, since colligative formulas are also derived from vapour pressure reasoning
questions.explanation: Strictly, 'ideal solution' (as defined via Raoult's law holding exactly at all compositions, with zero enthalpy/volume change on mixing) is a concept built for two-volatile-component liquid mixtures. Van't Hoff factor problems (electrolytes, associating solutes) are usually dilute solutions of a typically non-volatile solute, analysed via the dilute-solution colligative-property formulas (ΔT<sub>b</sub>, ΔT<sub>f</sub>, π, relative lowering), with i simply included as a multiplicative correction -- a related but distinct application of the same underlying vapour-pressure ideas.
questions.hint: Recall that 'ideal solution' in the strict Raoult's-law sense is specifically about two volatile liquids across the whole composition range; van't Hoff factor problems are almost always about a single dilute (often non-volatile) solute.
distractor_logic: Van't Hoff factor problems are a completely standard part of liquid-solution colligative-property analysis (e.g. aqueous NaCl solutions), not restricted to gaseous systems.

All of these dilute-solution colligative-property formulas (ΔT<sub>b</sub>, ΔT<sub>f</sub>, RLVP, π) are themselves derived from vapour pressure/Raoult's law reasoning, so the two topics are certainly related.

The strict 'ideal solution' label (full-range Raoult's law, zero mixing enthalpy/volume) is not typically how dilute electrolyte/associating-solute problems are classified, even though both trace back to vapour pressure reasoning.

Actual ΔT<sub>b</sub> ≈ 0.052 K, versus 0.099 K predicted for a non-dissociating solute

questions.question: A solution shows a freezing point depression of 0.372 K in water (K<sub>f</sub> = 1.86 K kg mol<sup>−1</sup>). Given that pure water's vapour pressure at this temperature is 23.8 mmHg, and using the dilute approximation x<sub>2</sub> ≈ m × M<sub>1</sub>/1000 (with M<sub>1</sub> = 18 g mol<sup>−1</sup> for water), what is the approximate vapour pressure of this solution?

topics.name: Types of Solutions and Concentration Terms
topics.summary: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more substances, made of a solvent (present in larger amount) and one or more solutes. For binary solutions the solvent and solute can each be solid, liquid, or gas, giving nine possible types (e.g. sugar in water = solid-in-liquid; soda water = gas-in-liquid; alloys = solid-in-solid). Concentration expresses how much solute is present per unit of solvent or solution, and NCERT uses several interconvertible measures: mass percentage (mass of solute ÷ mass of solution × 100), volume percentage, mass by volume percentage, parts per million (ppm) for trace amounts, mole fraction (moles of one component ÷ total moles, always between 0 and 1, and the mole fractions of all components sum to 1), molarity (moles of solute per litre of solution, mol L-1, temperature-dependent because volume changes with temperature), and molality (moles of solute per kg of solvent, mol kg-1, temperature-independent because it is mass-based). Molality and mole fraction are preferred for colligative-property calculations precisely because they do not change with temperature.
key_formulas: Mass % = (mass of solute ÷ mass of solution) × 100
Mole fraction x<sub>A</sub> = n<sub>A</sub> ÷ (n<sub>A</sub> + n<sub>B</sub>); Σx<sub>i</sub> = 1
Molarity (M) = moles of solute ÷ volume of solution (L)
Molality (m) = moles of solute ÷ mass of solvent (kg)
ppm = (mass of solute ÷ mass of solution) × 10<sup>6</sup>
topics.worked_example: 18 g of glucose (molar mass 180 g mol-1) is dissolved in 500 g of water. Moles of glucose = 18 ÷ 180 = 0.1 mol. Molality = 0.1 mol ÷ 0.5 kg = 0.2 mol kg-1. If the solution density is 1.02 g mL-1 and total mass is 518 g, volume = 518 ÷ 1.02 ≈ 507.8 mL = 0.5078 L, so Molarity = 0.1 ÷ 0.5078 ≈ 0.197 mol L-1 — note molarity and molality are close but not identical here, and only become numerically equal in very dilute aqueous solutions where density ≈ 1 g mL-1.
common_mistakes: Using mass of solution instead of mass of solvent when calculating molality (molality needs solvent mass only)
Forgetting that molarity changes with temperature (volume expands) while molality does not (mass is temperature-independent)
Treating mole fraction as a percentage instead of a pure ratio between 0 and 1

topics.name: Solubility of Gases in Liquids (Henry's Law)
topics.summary: Henry's law describes the solubility of a gas in a liquid: the partial pressure of the gas in the vapour phase is directly proportional to the mole fraction of the gas dissolved in the solution, p = KH·x, where KH is the Henry's law constant (units of pressure). A higher KH at a given partial pressure means lower solubility, since x = p ÷ KH. KH increases with temperature for most gases, which is why gas solubility in water decreases as temperature rises (fish are more stressed in warm water; aquatic organisms prefer cold water for higher dissolved O2). Practical applications include the discomfort of low O2 partial pressure at high altitude, the use of high-pressure O2/He mixtures to avoid excess N2 dissolving in a scuba diver's blood (preventing 'the bends' from N2 bubbles on ascent), and the fizz of carbonated drinks (CO2 bottled under high pressure escapes as pressure drops on opening). Henry's law only holds for gases that do not react chemically with the solvent, and only at low to moderate pressures.
key_formulas: p = K<sub>H</sub> × x (Henry's law)
x<sub>gas</sub> = p<sub>gas</sub> ÷ K<sub>H</sub>
Moles dissolved n = x<sub>gas</sub> × n<sub>solvent</sub> (dilute solution, x<sub>gas</sub> small)
topics.worked_example: The partial pressure of CO2 at 298 K over a solution is 0.835 bar, and KH for CO2 in water at 298 K is 1.67 × 103 bar. Mole fraction of CO2 dissolved: x = p ÷ KH = 0.835 ÷ 1670 ≈ 5.0 × 10-4. If this solution contains 1 L (≈ 55.5 mol) of water, moles of CO2 ≈ x × 55.5 ≈ 0.0278 mol, i.e. about 1.22 g of dissolved CO2 per litre.
common_mistakes: Inverting the relationship and using x = K<sub>H</sub> ÷ p instead of x = p ÷ K<sub>H</sub>
Assuming higher K<sub>H</sub> means higher solubility, when it actually means lower solubility at the same pressure
Applying Henry's law to gases that react with the solvent (e.g. NH<sub>3</sub> or HCl in water), where it does not hold

topics.name: Vapour Pressure of Solutions and Raoult's Law
topics.summary: Raoult's law states that for a solution of volatile liquids, the partial vapour pressure of each component is proportional to its mole fraction in the liquid phase: pA = p°A·xA, where p°A is the vapour pressure of pure A. The total vapour pressure of the solution is the sum of the partial pressures, ptotal = p°AxA + p°BxB. In the vapour phase above the solution, the component with the higher vapour pressure (more volatile) is proportionally richer than it was in the liquid — this is the basis of fractional distillation. Raoult's law applies to volatile solutes as well as solvents; when the solute is non-volatile, its p° is effectively 0, and only the solvent contributes to the vapour pressure, which is the starting point for the relative-lowering-of-vapour-pressure colligative property. For gases dissolved in liquids, Henry's law is a special case of the same idea, with p° replaced by KH.
key_formulas: p<sub>A</sub> = p°<sub>A</sub> × x<sub>A</sub> (Raoult's law, component A)
p<sub>total</sub> = p°<sub>A</sub>x<sub>A</sub> + p°<sub>B</sub>x<sub>B</sub> (two volatile liquids)
Mole fraction of A in vapour, y<sub>A</sub> = p<sub>A</sub> ÷ p<sub>total</sub>
topics.worked_example: Pure benzene has p° = 150 mm Hg and pure toluene has p° = 50 mm Hg at a given temperature. For a solution with xbenzene = 0.6 and xtoluene = 0.4: pbenzene = 150 × 0.6 = 90 mm Hg; ptoluene = 50 × 0.4 = 20 mm Hg. ptotal = 90 + 20 = 110 mm Hg. Mole fraction of benzene in the vapour = 90 ÷ 110 ≈ 0.818 — richer in benzene than the liquid (0.6), confirming benzene (the more volatile component) enriches the vapour phase.
common_mistakes: Using the liquid-phase mole fraction directly as the vapour-phase mole fraction (they differ except at azeotropes)
Forgetting to multiply by mole fraction and just adding the two pure vapour pressures
Applying Raoult's law to a non-volatile solute's own partial pressure instead of treating it as zero

topics.name: Ideal and Non-Ideal Solutions
topics.summary: An ideal solution obeys Raoult's law over the entire concentration range, with ΔmixH = 0 (no heat absorbed or released on mixing) and ΔmixV = 0 (no volume change on mixing), because solute-solvent interactions are essentially identical in strength to solute-solute and solvent-solvent interactions. Examples include n-hexane and n-heptane, or benzene and toluene. Real solutions that deviate show either positive deviation (A-B interactions weaker than A-A/B-B, so the components escape more easily than Raoult's law predicts: ptotal > ideal value, ΔmixH > 0 endothermic, ΔmixV > 0; e.g. ethanol-acetone, carbon disulphide-acetone) or negative deviation (A-B interactions stronger than A-A/B-B, e.g. new hydrogen bonding: ptotal < ideal value, ΔmixH < 0 exothermic, ΔmixV < 0; e.g. chloroform-acetone, HCl-water). At certain compositions, strongly deviating mixtures form azeotropes — constant-boiling mixtures that distil without change in composition (minimum-boiling azeotrope for positive deviation, e.g. ethanol-water 95.6% ethanol; maximum-boiling azeotrope for negative deviation, e.g. HCl-water 20.2% HCl), which cannot be separated by simple fractional distillation.
key_formulas: Ideal: p<sub>A</sub> = p°<sub>A</sub>x<sub>A</sub>, p<sub>B</sub> = p°<sub>B</sub>x<sub>B</sub>; Δ<sub>mix</sub>H = 0; Δ<sub>mix</sub>V = 0
Positive deviation: p<sub>total</sub> > p°<sub>A</sub>x<sub>A</sub> + p°<sub>B</sub>x<sub>B</sub>; Δ<sub>mix</sub>H > 0
Negative deviation: p<sub>total</sub> < p°<sub>A</sub>x<sub>A</sub> + p°<sub>B</sub>x<sub>B</sub>; Δ<sub>mix</sub>H < 0
topics.worked_example: Ethanol and acetone are mixed. Because ethanol's O–H···O hydrogen bonding with itself is disrupted by acetone (which cannot hydrogen-bond as strongly back), the A-B attraction is weaker than the original A-A/B-B attractions. Molecules escape into vapour more easily than Raoult's law predicts, so the observed total vapour pressure is higher than the calculated ideal value — a positive deviation, consistent with ΔmixH being slightly positive (endothermic) and ΔmixV being slightly positive (volume expands on mixing).
common_mistakes: Mixing up which deviation goes with which sign of Δ<sub>mix</sub>H (positive deviation = endothermic, weaker new interactions, not stronger)
Assuming all non-ideal mixtures form azeotropes; only sufficiently strong deviations do so at specific compositions
Thinking azeotropes are pure compounds; they are mixtures with a fixed distillate composition, not compounds with a fixed formula

topics.name: Relative Lowering of Vapour Pressure
topics.summary: When a non-volatile solute is dissolved in a solvent, the vapour pressure of the solution is lower than that of the pure solvent, because solute molecules occupy some of the surface and reduce the solvent's escaping tendency. The relative lowering of vapour pressure is (p° − ps) ÷ p°, and for a dilute solution of a non-volatile, non-electrolyte solute this equals the mole fraction of the solute, xsolute — this is one of Raoult's law's most important consequences and forms the basis for experimentally determining a solute's molar mass. It is a true colligative property (depends only on the number of solute particles, not their identity) only when the solute does not dissociate or associate and is non-volatile; for volatile solutes or electrolytes the simple xsolute relation needs the van't Hoff correction factor i, or does not apply directly because the solute itself contributes vapour pressure.
key_formulas: (p° − p<sub>s</sub>) ÷ p° = x<sub>solute</sub> = n<sub>solute</sub> ÷ (n<sub>solute</sub> + n<sub>solvent</sub>)
For dilute solution: x<sub>solute</sub> ≈ n<sub>solute</sub> ÷ n<sub>solvent</sub> = (w<sub>2</sub>/M<sub>2</sub>) ÷ (w<sub>1</sub>/M<sub>1</sub>)
M<sub>2</sub> (solute molar mass) = (w<sub>2</sub> × M<sub>1</sub> × p°) ÷ (w<sub>1</sub> × (p° − p<sub>s</sub>)), dilute limit
topics.worked_example: 18 g glucose (M = 180 g mol-1) is dissolved in 180 g water (M = 18 g mol-1) at a temperature where pure water's vapour pressure p° = 17.5 mm Hg. nglucose = 0.1 mol, nwater = 10 mol. xglucose = 0.1 ÷ 10.1 ≈ 0.0099. Relative lowering = (p° − ps) ÷ p° ≈ 0.0099, so p° − ps ≈ 0.0099 × 17.5 ≈ 0.173 mm Hg, giving ps ≈ 17.33 mm Hg.
common_mistakes: Using x<sub>solvent</sub> instead of x<sub>solute</sub> on the right-hand side of the relative-lowering equation
Applying the simple relation directly to an electrolyte solute without including the van't Hoff factor i
Confusing 'relative lowering' (a dimensionless fraction) with the absolute lowering p° − p<sub>s</sub> (a pressure)

topics.name: Elevation of Boiling Point
topics.summary: The boiling point of a solution containing a non-volatile solute is higher than that of the pure solvent, because the reduced vapour pressure means a higher temperature is needed to raise the vapour pressure to atmospheric pressure. This is the elevation of boiling point, ΔTb = Tb(solution) − Tb(pure solvent), and for dilute solutions it is directly proportional to the molality of the solution, ΔTb = Kb·m, where Kb is the molal elevation constant (ebullioscopic constant, K kg mol-1) — a property of the solvent alone, independent of the solute. For water, Kb = 0.52 K kg mol-1. Since ΔTb depends only on the number of solute particles, it is a colligative property, and measuring it allows determination of a solute's molar mass. Solvents with larger Kb values show more pronounced boiling-point elevation for the same molality, which is why Kb varies significantly across different solvents.
key_formulas: ΔT<sub>b</sub> = K<sub>b</sub> × m (molality)
m = (w<sub>2</sub> × 1000) ÷ (M<sub>2</sub> × w<sub>1</sub>), w<sub>1</sub> in g
M<sub>2</sub> (molar mass of solute) = (K<sub>b</sub> × w<sub>2</sub> × 1000) ÷ (ΔT<sub>b</sub> × w<sub>1</sub>)
topics.worked_example: 1.5 g of a non-volatile, non-electrolyte solute (M = 60 g mol-1) is dissolved in 50 g of water (Kb = 0.52 K kg mol-1). Moles of solute = 1.5 ÷ 60 = 0.025 mol. Molality = 0.025 ÷ 0.050 kg = 0.5 mol kg-1. ΔTb = 0.52 × 0.5 = 0.26 K, so the solution boils at 100.26 °C instead of 100 °C.
common_mistakes: Using mass of solution instead of mass of solvent (in grams, converted to kg) when computing molality for ΔT<sub>b</sub>
Forgetting to multiply by the van't Hoff factor i for electrolyte solutes, understating ΔT<sub>b</sub>
Treating K<sub>b</sub> as a universal constant rather than a solvent-specific property that differs between solvents

topics.name: Depression of Freezing Point
topics.summary: The freezing point of a solution is lower than that of the pure solvent, because the solution's vapour pressure curve is shifted down, meeting the solid solvent's vapour pressure curve at a lower temperature. This is the depression of freezing point, ΔTf = Tf(pure solvent) − Tf(solution), proportional to molality for dilute solutions: ΔTf = Kf·m, where Kf is the molal depression constant (cryoscopic constant, K kg mol-1), a solvent property. For water, Kf = 1.86 K kg mol-1. Freezing-point depression is the principle behind spreading salt or CaCl2 on icy roads (lowers the freezing point of the water-ice mixture so ice melts at sub-zero temperatures) and adding ethylene glycol antifreeze to car radiators to prevent the coolant from freezing in winter. Like ΔTb, ΔTf is a colligative property useful for determining unknown molar masses, and for electrolytes the observed ΔTf is larger than predicted from molality alone due to the van't Hoff factor.
key_formulas: ΔT<sub>f</sub> = K<sub>f</sub> × m (molality)
m = (w<sub>2</sub> × 1000) ÷ (M<sub>2</sub> × w<sub>1</sub>), w<sub>1</sub> in g
M<sub>2</sub> (molar mass of solute) = (K<sub>f</sub> × w<sub>2</sub> × 1000) ÷ (ΔT<sub>f</sub> × w<sub>1</sub>)
topics.worked_example: 2.5 g of a non-electrolyte solute is dissolved in 100 g of water (Kf = 1.86 K kg mol-1), and the freezing point drops by 0.372 K. m = ΔTf ÷ Kf = 0.372 ÷ 1.86 = 0.2 mol kg-1. Moles of solute = 0.2 × 0.100 kg = 0.02 mol. M2 = 2.5 ÷ 0.02 = 125 g mol-1.
common_mistakes: Swapping K<sub>b</sub> and K<sub>f</sub> values for water (0.52 vs 1.86) between boiling-point and freezing-point problems
Forgetting the van't Hoff factor for ionic solutes, leading to an underestimated predicted ΔT<sub>f</sub>
Using mass of solution instead of solvent mass in the molality calculation

topics.name: Osmosis and Osmotic Pressure
topics.summary: Osmosis is the spontaneous flow of solvent molecules through a semipermeable membrane from a region of lower solute concentration (or pure solvent) into a region of higher solute concentration, until equilibrium is reached or is prevented by applying external pressure. The osmotic pressure (π) is the minimum external pressure that must be applied to the solution side to just stop this net solvent flow; for dilute solutions it obeys an equation analogous to the ideal gas law, πV = nRT, so π = CRT where C is molarity. Osmotic pressure is a colligative property and is especially useful for determining the molar mass of large molecules (e.g. proteins, polymers) because even small concentrations produce a measurably large π. Two solutions with the same osmotic pressure at a given temperature are called isotonic; if one has higher π it is hypertonic and the other hypotonic relative to it. Reverse osmosis applies pressure greater than the osmotic pressure to force solvent to flow against its natural direction (from concentrated to dilute side), used in desalination and water purification, typically through a cellulose acetate membrane.
key_formulas: π = CRT = (n ÷ V) × R × T
M<sub>2</sub> (solute molar mass) = (w<sub>2</sub>RT) ÷ (πV)
Isotonic solutions: π<sub>1</sub> = π<sub>2</sub> at the same T
topics.worked_example: 1 g of a protein is dissolved in 200 mL of solution, and the osmotic pressure at 300 K is found to be 2.57 × 10-3 atm (R = 0.0821 L atm K-1 mol-1). n = πV ÷ RT = (2.57 × 10-3 × 0.2) ÷ (0.0821 × 300) ≈ 2.086 × 10-5 mol. Molar mass = 1 ÷ 2.086 × 10-5 ≈ 47,940 g mol-1 — illustrating why osmotic pressure (not ΔTf or ΔTb, which would be immeasurably tiny) is used for large biomolecules.
common_mistakes: Using T in °C instead of Kelvin in π = CRT
Forgetting to convert volume to litres before applying πV = nRT
Confusing which of two solutions is hypertonic vs hypotonic (higher π = hypertonic, not hypotonic)

topics.name: Abnormal Molar Mass and van't Hoff Factor
topics.summary: Colligative properties (relative lowering of vapour pressure, ΔTb, ΔTf, π) depend on the number of particles of solute in solution, not their chemical identity. When a solute dissociates into ions (e.g. NaCl → Na+ + Cl-) or associates into larger units (e.g. acetic acid dimerising in benzene via hydrogen bonding), the observed colligative effect deviates from that predicted assuming the solute stays as single molecules, producing an abnormal molar mass (lower than expected for dissociation, higher than expected for association). Van't Hoff introduced a correction factor, i, defined as the ratio of the observed colligative property (or observed number of particles) to the value calculated assuming no dissociation/association. i > 1 for dissociation (i = 1 + (n − 1)α for n ions per formula unit with degree of dissociation α); i < 1 for association (i = 1 + ((1/n) − 1)α for association into n-mers with degree of association α); i = 1 for a solute that neither dissociates nor associates. Every colligative property equation gets multiplied by i when dissociation or association occurs (e.g. π = iCRT, ΔTb = iKbm).
key_formulas: i = observed colligative property ÷ calculated (normal) colligative property = normal molar mass ÷ observed (abnormal) molar mass
Dissociation: i = 1 + (n − 1)α, n = number of ions/particles produced
Association: i = 1 + ((1/n) − 1)α, n = number of units associating
ΔT<sub>f</sub> = iK<sub>f</sub>m; ΔT<sub>b</sub> = iK<sub>b</sub>m; π = iCRT
topics.worked_example: 0.1 mol kg-1 aqueous KCl solution has an observed ΔTf of 0.352 K (Kf = 1.86 K kg mol-1). Normal (undissociated) ΔTf would be Kfm = 1.86 × 0.1 = 0.186 K. i = 0.352 ÷ 0.186 ≈ 1.89. Since KCl gives n = 2 ions on complete dissociation, i = 1 + (2 − 1)α = 1 + α, so α ≈ 0.89, i.e. about 89% dissociated at this concentration — close to, but not exactly, complete dissociation.
common_mistakes: Using the wrong sign/direction in the association formula (i < 1 for association, i > 1 for dissociation, not the reverse)
Forgetting to include i in colligative-property equations for known electrolytes or associating solutes
Computing α without correctly identifying n (number of ions or units) for the specific solute in the problem
